Case report: A rare case of malignant solitary fibrous tumor within the joint cavity with review of the literature
Solitary fibrous tumors (SFTs) are classified as fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumors that originate from CD34-positive dendritic cells and usually occur in the pleura. In this paper, we describe a case of SFT within the joint cavity of the left knee. A 60-year-old man was admitted to hospital due to swelling in the left knee for the past 8 months without relevant trauma history. X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) presented a large, ill-circumscribed, hypervascular, and highly enhanced mass with eccentric calcification and peripheral, intra-lesional vessels. Subsequently, the patient underwent surgical resection. Postoperative pathology confirmed the neoplastic cells to be positive for CD34, Bcl-2, and SATA6, therefore was finally diagnosed as malignant SFT. The patient developed bone metastases within 1 year after surgery. SFT in the joint cavity is rare, and it is difficult to make a preoperative diagnosis.

Introduction

Klemperer and Rabin reported the first case of a fibrous mesothelioma located in the pleura and showed a benign clinical course (1). The understanding of solitary fibrous tumors (SFTs) has evolved over time. According to the recent World Health Organization (WHO) classification of soft tissue tumors, SFTs are classified as fibroblastic/myofibroblastic tumors that originate from CD34-positive dendritic cells, the biological behavior of which is further subdivided into intermediate/locally aggressive (SFT-benign), intermediate/rarely metastasizing (SFT-NOS, including fat-forming SFT and giant cell-rich SFT), and malignant (SFT-malignant) (2). Hemangiopericytoma was once used as a synonym for SFT occurring extra-pleura. Subsequently, giant cell angiofibroma and hemangiopericytoma were removed from the WHO classification of soft tissue tumors in 2013, with the former being classified as SFT outside the pleura, which was described as one morphologic variant, while the latter was recommended to be disregarded as a lot of soft tissue tumors could display a hemangiopericytomatous vasculature (3, 4). In addition, the NAB2–STAT6 gene fusion was identified in SFTs in 2013 (5).SFTs are relatively rarely seen in clinical practice, but occur in a wide variety of body sites (6–9). With regard to the imaging features of SFTs, there are no characteristic findings. Computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), echocardiography, and positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) imaging findings have been reported mainly in case series (10). Radiographs, echocardiography, and CT alone generally yield non-specific findings for SFTs, and the density of SFTs can be uniform or uneven. At ultrasound, SFTs are typically hypoechoic, but are occasionally heterogeneous. Calcification is rare, but could exist and can be observed using CT or by detecting the presence of bright echo-dense areas on echocardiography. Compared with those of CT, the imaging findings of MRI are more conducive to helping radiologists in analysis and assessment due to their high resolution of soft tissue and multi-parameter imaging. MRI can reflect the histological characteristics of SFTs. Low-signal-intensity foci on T1- and T2-weighted images, representing the collagen content, are a frequent feature of SFTs. As highly vascular tumors, SFTs are avidly enhanced on both CT and MRI. Whole-body imaging with PET-CT can be performed to determine multiple tumor sites and to detect metastatic lesions in the case of malignant SFTs. An increased uptake of fluorodeoxyglucose F18 (F-18 FDG), which corresponds to glucose metabolism, could indicate an aggressive or a malignant type of SFT (10, 11).In this paper, we present a case of a malignant SFT within the joint cavity of the left knee, a rare site of occurrence, and the morphology of the mass led to this case being rare. We mainly focused on its radiological features, followed by a review of the literature. It is hoped that the study findings will be beneficial to radiologists in clinical work.

Case presentation

Ethics approval for this study was granted by the Institutional Review Board of our hospital. A 60-year-old man was admitted to the Department of Orthopedics of our hospital due to swelling in the left knee for the past 8 months. The patient had no history of relevant trauma and had no other complaints of discomfort. The skin and the temperature of the left knee were normal. X-ray of the left knee was first taken (
Figure 1
), which showed soft tissue swelling mainly on the anteromedial side of the knee, where the density was higher than that of normal soft tissue. Moreover, some strip calcification could be seen in the X-ray, but there was no destruction of the bone. To further define the lesion, the radiologist recommended CT or MRI. Enhanced CT and MRI were both performed, which confirmed the irregular soft tissue mass within the joint cavity of the left knee. CT of the left knee (
Figure 2
) showed that the calcification in the mass was mainly located at the edge. After injection of a contrast material, the enhancement was heterogeneous, and a nodular enhancement of the lesion was presented. Small enhanced vessels could be seen in and around the mass. There was no destruction to the adjacent bones. MRI presented the shape of the lesion better (
Figure 3
). The mass was irregular, and it appeared to grow along the synovial membrane of the joint and was partly nodular. On T2-weighted images (T2WI), the lesion was hyperintense. On T1-weighted images (T1WI), the lesion was mainly hypointense, but with some nodular hyperintensity. In the enhanced images, the lesion showed a markedly heterogeneous enhancement, especially the nodules. The margin of the lesion was unclear. The adjacent medial collateral ligament of the left knee was swollen and was partly invaded by the mass. Edema was evident in the soft tissue surrounding the mass. It was difficult to determine what the lesion was; therefore, a needle biopsy was performed, which suggested malignancy. F-18 FDG PET-CT, which was performed for tumor restaging, revealed active heterogeneous enhancement of only one tumor, with a maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax) of 7.51 (
Figure 4
). No other metabolically active lesions were seen in the body; therefore, the patient underwent surgical resection. The soft tissue and muscle around the tumor were separated, and the distal femur and the proximal tibia and fibula were excised for complete resection of the tumor. Subsequently, knee prosthesis replacement was performed. The whole operation was successful. Postoperative pathology confirmed malignant SFT with focal necrosis. Immunohistochemical examination revealed that the neoplastic cells were positive for CD34, Bcl-2, and SATA6 (
Supplementary Figure S1
). The immunohistochemistry results were as follows: CD34 (partially ++), Bcl-2 (partially ++), STAT6 (weak +), EMA (focal +), desmin (−), S-100 (−), beta-catenin (focal +), SMA (focal +), CK(AE1/AE3) (scattered +), CAM5.2 (scattered +), and Ki-67 (30% +). Approximately 11 months after surgery, the patient came to our hospital again due to bone abnormalities, and it was confirmed by imaging examination and puncture pathology that the patient had multiple bone metastases (
Supplementary Figure S2
).

Discussion

SFTs are rare tumors accounting for less than 2% of soft tissue tumors (12, 13). SFTs most commonly occur in the pleura, but approximately 10%–25% can derive from soft tissues, most commonly in the proximal lower limbs, usually deep. In terms of the imaging features of SFTs, they commonly present as large, well-circumscribed, hypervascular masses deep to fascia along major neurovascular bundles (14). In this report, we described a rare case of a malignant SFT within the joint cavity of the left knee.At present, imaging findings of SFTs in soft tissue are mainly presented as individual or small case series reports (14–30). To our knowledge, the largest case series published to date is that by Swami et al., which showed the MRI features of 39 patients (14). The existing literature on the imaging features of SFTs in soft tissue usually describe them as located in the lower extremity and often deep to fascia along major neurovascular bundles. A small proportion of SFTs can occur in superficial sites, such as the abdominal wall. The case reported here occurred in the left lower limb, which was consistent with previous reports; however, its growth was mainly located in the cavity of the knee joint. Garcia-Bennett et al. previously reported on the case of a 77-year-old female patient with SFT (29) whose tumor affected the intra- and extra-articular fat with disruption of the medial patellar retinaculum of the knee. However, unlike that in our case, the tumor mainly grew in the intra-articular space, which is extremely rare and, to our knowledge, has not been previously reported. Most SFTs presented a well-defined lobulated mass in previous studies (14). In our case, however, the tumor did not have a clump-like shape. It was ill-defined and appeared more like a mass growing along the intraluminal synovium, which may be an indication of its malignancy. The rare site of occurrence and the morphology of the mass led to this being a rare case. On MRI, there were various results of T1 and T2 signal presentation of SFT in soft tissue reported. On T2WI, most studies described SFTs as heterogeneous, but predominantly hyperintense (26, 27), while some were described as heterogeneous with mixed hyper- and hypointense signals (28, 29). On T1WI, a number of studies described SFTs as isointense to muscle (26–28), while others were described as isointense-to-hypointense (23) or isointense-to-hyperintense (29). The diversity of the MRI signal features on T1- and T2-weighted imaging could be due to the influence of the tumor cellular variant composition, which was difficult to characterize in previous studies. In our case, the tumor was heterogeneous, with mixed hypointense and hyperintense signals on both T1- and T2-weighted imaging. In the fluid-sensitive sequences, a feature resembling morphologic internal lobulations with intra-lesional low-T2 signal bands/septations on a background of heterogenous signal was demonstrated (
Figure 3
), which we believed might be the “human brain” or the “pseudo-cerebriform” sign on the T2/STIR-weighted fat-suppressed MRI acquisitions, as Swami et al. reported (14).Soft tissue SFTs are classically described as hypervascular lesions; however, a number of studies found a feature of peripheral extracapsular vessels forming an apparent vascular pedicle, which was thought to more likely occur in larger lesions. This was observed not only in SFTs of soft tissue (14, 26, 29), but also of the pleura and retroperitoneum (31–33). Some studies recommended the feature of large collateral feeding vessels at a vascular pedicle as a possible distinguishing feature of SFTs compared with other hypervascular masses (27, 29), but its diagnostic specificity has not been carefully assessed. In our case, the peripheral and intra-lesional vessels were enhanced on CT imaging, and there were many large collateral feeding vessels around the mass, which was similar to previous studies to a certain extent. The enhancement pattern of soft tissue SFTs is often heterogeneous (14, 26–29, 34, 35), reflecting the high degree of vascularity. Some internal areas without enhancement, after injection of a contrast medium, corresponded with high signals on T1 and T2 images. We believed they might represent areas of tumor necrosis in histology.Calcification is rare in SFTs. In our case, the calcification was patchy and located at the edge of the mass, which made it more difficult to distinguish from synovial sarcoma, which typically presents as a mass around large joints with obvious mixed signals and eccentric calcification occurring in young adults. Different forms of calcification in SFTs have been reported previously, including tiny, scattered, partial, or prominent calcification (27, 36, 37). Some researchers believe that calcification could be regarded as an indicator of malignancy (38), but its reliability has not been proven. In our case, the F-18 FDG PET-CT showed good uptake in the primary tumor and no other lesions were detected, which helped in the staging. There are only a few descriptions in the literature with regard to the PET manifestations of SFTs. It was found that benign SFTs exhibit low-grade activity in PET and that malignant SFTs tend to be strongly hypermetabolic and homogeneous (10).The standard treatment for SFTs is still radical resection with long-term follow-up due to 5%–10% of patients experiencing recurrence or metastasis. The fifth edition of WHO recommended the use of a risk stratification model modified by Demicco et al. (39), which includes age (<55 years or ≥55 years), tumor size (<5, 5–10, 10–15 cm, or ≥15 cm), mitotic count (0, 1–3, or ≥4 per 10 high-magnification fields), and tumor necrosis (<10% or ≥10%). The scores are then added together to create a risk rating: 0–3 points for low risk, 4–5 points for moderate risk, and 6–7 points for high risk. According to this criterion, our patient had a total score of 7, indicating a high risk of metastasis. Adjuvant radiotherapy can be considered for high-risk, inoperable, or locally recurrent lesion, but its survival benefit is still under investigation. The patient in this study did not receive radiotherapy after surgery. Unfortunately, 11 months after surgery, the patient developed bone metastases. Ultimately, benign SFTs have a local recurrence rate of 8%, and malignant lesions recur within 2 years in as many as 63% of cases (40).

Conclusions

We reported on a relatively uncommon case of malignant SFT within the joint cavity of the left knee, which presented as a large, ill-circumscribed, hypervascular mass with eccentric calcification and was diagnosed by immunohistochemical examination as positive for CD34, Bcl-2, and SATA6. The patient developed bone metastases within 1 year after surgery. This is the first case of SFT in the joint cavity, and radiologists should be aware of the possibility of this rare origin. Soft tissue SFTs are difficult to diagnose and should be carefully followed up after surgery.

PMC11570904.raw_case:
Adult-onset pancreatic neuroblastoma: A case report with a literature review
Neuroblastoma is an aggressive malignancy commonly found in children, with adult patients being quite rare. Pancreatic neuroblastoma, even among adult cases, is especially rare. We present a case of a 26-year-old woman presented with mild abdominal pain and a palpable mass diagnosed as neuroblastoma affecting the pancreas. After initial diagnostic challenges, a biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of neuroblastoma. The patient thereafter underwent a course of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, followed by a complex surgical resection. This case highlights the importance of a comprehensive diagnostic approach, including repeated biopsies and the involvement of a multidisciplinary team in the management of rare presentations of adult neuroblastoma.

Introduction

Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor that originates from neural crest cells and is commonly found in infants and young children. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor in children but is rare in adults [1]. Diagnosing and treating adult neuroblastoma can be particularly challenging, especially in high-risk cases that have poorer outcomes. Roughly half of neuroblastoma cases are classified as high-risk cases, especially in individuals over 18 months old with (stage M) metastatic disease and genetic indicators like MYCN amplification, resulting in decreased survival rates [2,3].As neuroblastoma usually starts in the adrenal glands or around the sympathetic chain, it can sometimes involve the pancreas, as seen in a few adult cases. Diagnosing pancreatic neuroblastoma can be difficult because it often resembles other types of pancreatic tumors, making identification more complicated [4,5].In this case, we describe a 26-year-old woman who first came with a challenging-to-diagnose abdominal mass. After being referred to our hospital, she went through a comprehensive diagnostic workup, which finally resulted in the diagnosis of neuroblastoma of the pancreas. The patient received both medical and surgical management, starting with neoadjuvant chemotherapy before undergoing a complex surgery. This report covers the challenges in diagnosis, treatment approaches, and distinct manifestations of neuroblastoma in an adult patient, focusing on the pancreas and reviewing relevant studies to highlight the rare occurrence and management of neuroblastoma in adults.

Case presentation

A 26-year-old female presented to the clinic with a 3-month history of dull, mild abdominal pain localized to the epigastric region without radiation. She also reported feeling a hard mass in the area of pain but declined any associated symptoms such as weight loss, nausea, changes in bowel habits, or other gastrointestinal issues. On physical examination, an abdominal mass was palpable in the epigastric area and was tender to deep palpation. There were no signs of abdominal distention, and the rest of the abdominal examination was normal.Initial laboratory investigations showed mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL, while liver and renal function tests and electrolytes were within normal limits. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was conducted, which demonstrated bulky para-aortic and mesenteric lymphadenopathy, with the largest node measuring 37×36×30 mm. Also, hypo-dense enhancing lesions were observed in segments VI-VII of the right lobe of the liver, raising concerns for possible metastasis, and a biopsy was recommended.A biopsy was taken from the para-aortic and mesenteric lymph nodes, as well as the left ovary, omentum, liver, and peritoneum. The initial histopathology report revealed no evidence of malignancy, and a check of the slides at another laboratory proved this finding. Nevertheless, a second biopsy was performed, revealing a metastatic neuroectodermal tumor, likely a differentiating neuroblastoma. The patient was subsequently referred to our hospital, where the diagnosis was confirmed after comprehensively reviewing the slides.Additional imaging studies, including a PET-CT scan, demonstrated a potentially malignant hypermetabolic soft tissue mass in the right retroperitoneal pancreatic uncinated process and hypermetabolic mesenteric lymph nodes (Figs. 1 and 2). An MRI of the brain was also conducted to exclude metastasis, and fortunately, it revealed no signs of spreading to the brain.The patient began neoadjuvant chemotherapy according to the pediatric protocol for neuroblastoma. After completing chemotherapy, a follow-up PET-CT scan showed a regression in tumor size, indicating a positive response to the treatment. Following multidisciplinary team discussions, surgery was suggested. Preoperative planning with a CT scan showed the tumor's proximity to the superior mesenteric artery, posing significant surgical challenges,The surgery started with mobilizing the second part of the duodenum to assess the mass's respectability. Then, the mass was resected with a free margin, avoiding WIPPLE surgery. The peripancreatic and regional lymph nodes were also dissected.Despite the complexities, the surgery was successfully performed. Postoperatively, the patient experienced a pancreatic leak detected through amylase from the drain fluid. This complication was managed with octreotide 0.1 mg twice a day for a week, and the leak was resolved. The postoperative histopathology report confirmed the diagnosis of neuroblastoma and noted the changes induced by chemotherapy (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). A follow-up multislice CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast in the venous phase, performed after 6 months, indicates a reduction in the size of a well-defined retroperitoneal hypoenhancing lesion centered on the pancreatic uncinate process (Fig. 5).This case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges in treating neuroblastoma in an adult, a condition typically seen in pediatric patients. Despite the initial diagnostic difficulties, the patient responded well to chemotherapy and surgery, indicating a positive outcome.

Discussion

Neuroblastoma in adults is a rare and complex condition, significantly different from its pediatric counterpart in terms of diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis. This case emphasizes the many difficulties encountered when diagnosing and treating adult neuroblastoma, which is usually detected in advanced stages and can often resemble other abdominal or retroperitoneal malignancies [6].Diagnosing adult neuroblastoma is challenging. In this case, the initial biopsy failed to demonstrate malignancy, so another biopsy was needed to confirm the diagnosis. This reflects the common diagnostic challenges in adult neuroblastoma. Extensive imaging, such as PET-CT, was critical in identifying the disease's extent. In adults, neuroblastoma frequently presents with metastasis, as seen in this case with lymphadenopathy and liver involvement [[6], [7]]. Because it is rare, diagnostic delays are expected, highlighting the need for repeated and comprehensive investigations when initial results are inconclusive [8].The treatment options for neuroblastoma in adults are not standardized because most protocols are created for pediatric patients. In this case, the patient was treated with a pediatric chemotherapy protocol that led to tumor size reduction and facilitated surgical intervention. While chemotherapy can induce remission in adults, the general prognosis remains poor compared to pediatric patients [2,9]. Surgical resection, when possible, is regarded as the primary treatment. However, the complexity of surgery due to the tumor's location near vital structures, like the superior mesenteric artery in this case, makes the surgery very difficult. Despite the challenges, successful surgical resection can significantly improve the outcomes.Postoperative management is important, especially when complications occur, as seen with the pancreatic leak in this case. The management with octreotide allowed for successful resolution, highlighting the importance of vigilant postoperative care. Literature indicates that postoperative complications are more common in adult neuroblastoma patients than pediatric patients due to the complexity of the surgery, which necessitates a multidisciplinary approach to treatment [2,10].Neuroblastoma staging and risk stratification play a critical role in determining treatment and prognosis. The 2 main systems used for staging are the International Neuroblastoma Staging System (INSS) and the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group Staging System (INRGSS). The INSS, which is based on surgicopathologic findings, classifies tumors postoperatively. In contrast, the INRGSS uses imaging findings and is a pretreatment staging system. The INRGSS divides tumors into 4 stages (L1, L2, M, and MS) depending on the presence of image-defined risk factors (IDRFs), such as proximity to major blood vessels or organ [13,14]The INRGSS has significant implications for adults, as these staging systems allow for better comparison of treatment outcomes and prognostic evaluations across studies. This is crucial because adult neuroblastoma is often diagnosed in metastatic stages (INRGSS stage M), where treatment is particularly challenging and outcomes are poor. The use of these staging systems in adult cases could provide a clearer framework for prognosis and treatment strategies [13].The Curie scoring system also provides prognostic value, particularly for high-risk neuroblastoma patients. It is a semiquantitative scoring system based on the extent of mIBG-avid disease in 10 anatomic regions. A Curie score greater than 2 after induction therapy is linked with significantly worse event-free survival (EFS), highlighting its importance as a prognostic marker in managing advanced neuroblastoma cases [15].The prognosis for adult neuroblastoma is usually poor, with survival rates significantly lower than in pediatric patients. Most adults present with advanced-stage disease, often resistant to conventional chemotherapy, which leads to recurrences and a high mortality rate.However, the case discussed here demonstrates that adults who achieve complete remission following chemotherapy and surgical intervention can experience better long-term outcomes. Patients achieving complete remission after induction therapy could have superior progression-free survival and overall survival. However, these outcomes remain lower than those in children [2,11,12].A literature review revealed that pancreatic neuroblastoma in adults is extremely rare, with significant diagnostic and prognostic challenges. Abdou et al. [3] reported a case of a 22-year-old female with stroma-rich neuroblastoma in the pancreas who underwent a Whipple procedure and then, followed by chemotherapy, eventually died within 4 months. This highlights the aggressive nature of the condition and the difficulty in differentiating neuroblastoma from other pancreatic tumors. Immunohistochemical markers, such as neuropil and ganglionic differentiation, were critical to the diagnosis in the case.Rosenbaum et al. [5] analyzed a larger cohort, identifying pancreatic involvement in 7 neuroblastoma cases out of 1,031 patients. Most cases involved disease progression or recurrence, with imaging (CT and MIBG scintigraphy) playing a crucial role in detection. Pancreatic lesions were typically focal, though some cases showed diffuse infiltration. The prognosis was typically poor, reflecting the advanced stage of the disease at diagnosis and its aggressive nature in adults.Both studies highlight the rarity and poor outcomes of pancreatic neuroblastoma in adults, emphasizing the importance of early detection, comprehensive imaging, and a multidisciplinary treatment approach. Despite advances in diagnostic techniques, adult pancreatic neuroblastoma is still associated with a high recurrence rate and poor survival.This case highlights the diagnostic and therapeutic complexities of managing neuroblastoma in adults. The disease's rarity, aggressive nature, and resistance to typical treatment necessitate a tailored, multidisciplinary approach. While pediatric treatment protocols provide a foundation, adult-specific guidelines are urgently needed to improve outcomes. This case reveals that with aggressive management involving chemotherapy, surgery, and vigilant postoperative care, positive outcomes can be accomplished, though the prognosis for adult neuroblastoma remains guarded.

Conclusion

This case of pancreatic neuroblastoma in a 26-year-old female emphasizes the diagnostic challenges and the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in managing rare adult neuroblastoma cases. Despite the initial difficulties in diagnosis, the patient responded well to a combination of neoadjuvant chemotherapy and surgery, highlighting the potential for positive outcomes with aggressive and combined treatment. However, the prognosis for adult neuroblastoma remains poor, and more research is required to develop tailored therapeutic approaches for adult patients.

Patient consent

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for their anonymized information to be published in this article.

PMC11617941.raw_case:
Unusual presentation of a giant gluteal lipoma in a pediatric patient: Case report and clinical implications


Introduction and importance

Giant lipomas, particularly in pediatric patients and unusual locations like the gluteal region, are rare. These benign tumors can mimic other conditions, making diagnosis challenging. This case highlights the importance of considering giant lipomas in differential diagnoses and the challenges posed by delayed treatment.

Case presentation

A 14-year-old female presented with a large, firm mass in the gluteal region, which had grown over time. MRI showed a well-circumscribed mass without spinal involvement. The mass was surgically excised, and histopathology confirmed a benign lipoma.

Clinical discussion

This case demonstrates the diagnostic challenges of giant lipomas, especially when atypical in appearance. MRI was crucial for diagnosis and surgical planning. Early surgical excision is vital to prevent complications. The case also highlights the need for timely medical intervention, particularly in low-resource settings.

Conclusion

Early diagnosis and prompt surgical management are essential in cases of giant lipomas to prevent complications. Improved healthcare access and awareness in low-resource settings are necessary to ensure timely treatment.

Highlights

•Lipomas are composed of mature adipocytes and are typically slow-growing, painless, and usually asymptomatic.•Giant lipomas may mimic other dermatological or soft tissue conditions, further complicating diagnosis.•Histopathological examination is vital to confirm the diagnosis and rule out malignancy.•The management of giant lipomas involves a multidisciplinary approach, including thorough diagnostic evaluation.1

Introduction

Lipomas are the most common benign tumors of mesenchymal origin, accounting for approximately 16 % of all soft tissue tumors [1]. These tumors are composed of mature adipocytes and are typically slow-growing, painless, and asymptomatic [2]. Lipomas can develop in any area of the body where adipose tissue is present, though they are most frequently found in the upper part of the body, particularly on the trunk and neck [3]. Less commonly, lipomas may develop in atypical locations such as the gluteal region, hands, or even deeper within the body, including subfascial, parosteal, interosseous, or visceral sites [4]. Lipomas in these less common locations can be challenging to diagnose, particularly when they present as large or infiltrating tumors.In children, the incidence of lipomas is relatively low, and even more so for giant lipomas; defined as those with a diameter greater than 10 cm or a weight exceeding 200 g [5]. The occurrence of such large lipomas in pediatric patients, especially in unusual sites like the gluteal region, is extremely rare, making this case of a giant gluteal lipoma in a 14-year-old school girl a notable anomaly [6]. Giant lipomas may mimic other dermatological or soft tissue conditions, further complicating diagnosis [7].Epidemiologically, the exact incidence rate of giant lipomas is not well documented due to their rarity [8]. However, it is estimated that less than 5 % of all lipomas can be classified as giant lipomas [9]. A study reported an overall prevalence of lipomas at around 2.1 per 1000 individuals, with giant lipomas representing a small fraction of this group [2]. The study also highlighted that lipomas larger than 10 cm in size are uncommon, and those exceeding 20 cm are particularly rare.Lipomas can also be classified based on their location and tissue involvement. Subfascial lipomas may be further categorized into parosteal, interosseous, or visceral lipomas [10]. Among the visceral lipomas, those of the colon, for example, are usually localized at the submucosal level and are often asymptomatic, though they can cause complications such as bleeding, obstruction, or intussusception [11]. Adrenal myelolipomas are another rare type of visceral lipoma, which consists of an admixture of adipose tissue and hematopoietic elements within the adrenal glands, often detected incidentally through imaging [12]. Despite their varied presentations, most lipomas are small, encapsulated, and found in subcutaneous tissues, with sizes usually not exceeding 2 cm in diameter. However, when these tumors grow larger, they may become symptomatic and require surgical intervention [13].The gluteal region is an infrequent site for lipomas, with most cases occurring in more typical locations such as the trunk, neck, and upper extremities. The atypical presentation and location of a gluteal lipoma contribute to the clinical challenge in diagnosis, as large lipomas, particularly those in deep or less accessible regions, can mimic more serious conditions, including liposarcomas. This diagnostic uncertainty underscores the importance of thorough evaluation using imaging studies, particularly MRI, which plays a key role in the diagnostic workup by providing detailed information about the size, location, and characteristics of the tumor.MRI is especially useful in differentiating lipomas from other soft tissue tumors and is crucial for surgical planning [14]. In this case, the MRI showed a large, well-circumscribed mass without involvement of the spine, which is consistent with a benign lipoma but still required histological confirmation to rule out malignancy.Despite the benign nature of most lipomas, the clinical management of giant lipomas poses significant challenges, particularly when they occur in regions like the buttocks, where they can cause functional and cosmetic concerns. Surgical excision is often required, not only to confirm the diagnosis but also to relieve symptoms and prevent further growth. In this case, the successful excision of the mass was critical in alleviating the physical burden on the patient and preventing potential complications such as infection, ulceration, or even malignant transformation, although rare.The delay in presentation seen in this case is reflective of broader public health challenges. In many developing regions, access to healthcare is limited, and there is often a lack of awareness about the significance of early medical intervention for growing masses. Studies have shown that delays in seeking medical care are associated with increased morbidity and more complex surgical interventions. For example, a study from Nigeria highlighted that patients with large lipomas often presented late due to financial constraints and fear of surgery, leading to more extensive disease at the time of treatment [15].This case also underscores the importance of educating communities about the signs and symptoms of potentially serious conditions, even those that appear benign. Public health initiatives aimed at increasing awareness and improving access to healthcare services are essential in preventing such cases from progressing to advanced stages, where treatment becomes more complicated and outcomes less favorable.This work has been reported in line with the SCARE criteria [16].2

Case presentation

A 14-year-old female presented to our center with a progressively enlarging mass in the buttock region, extending to the lower back, over a period of about five years. The patient reported that the swelling began as a small lump and gradually increased in size. She denied any associated pain, skin changes, or discharge. There was no history of trauma or injury to the area, and no constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or neurological deficits were noted. The mass had grown significantly, affecting her ability to wear certain clothes and sit comfortably.On general examination, the patient was alert, with no pallor or jaundice, and exhibited a normal gait with stable vital signs. There were no palpable peripheral lymph nodes.On local examination, a large lobulated mass was observed, covering the entire buttock region and extending to the lower back, measuring 28 cm × 34 cm. The skin over the mass appeared normal in color and integrity (Fig. 1). The mass was non-tender, with multiple roots palpable at different positions on both the buttocks and lower back. It was partially mobile, not fixed to the underlying muscles, and firm in consistency. The mass extended over the anal opening but did not cause obstruction. A rectal examination revealed no abnormalities. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.Her laboratory investigations showed a white blood cell count of 6.07 × 109/L, hemoglobin of 12.6 g/dL, and a platelet count of 340 × 109/L. Serum creatinine was 30 μmol/L, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) was 3.22 mmol/L, potassium was 3.9 mmol/L, and sodium was 138.3 mmol/L. Rapid tests for HIV and syphilis were negative. An MRI scan revealed a large mass in the buttock region with no apparent connection to the spine and an unclear origin.The patient was scheduled for a wide local excision after obtaining informed consent from her caretaker. The procedure was successful, with the entire mass excised from its root and base (Fig. 2), and the specimen was sent for histopathological analysis. Her postoperative recovery was uneventful, and she was discharged eight days after surgery. Upon follow-up eight weeks later, the wound had healed well (Fig. 3), and there were no signs of recurrence. Histological examination of the excised tissue confirmed the diagnosis of a benign lipoma (Fig. 4).3

Discussion

In this particular case, the clinical presentation of the lipoma was very unusual, resembling a wart-like lesion, firm in consistency, and irregular surface. Such atypical presentations highlight the diagnostic challenges posed by giant lipomas, especially in pediatric patients. The mass was not only large but also deeply embedded in the gluteal region, making it less mobile and more difficult to distinguish from other types of soft tissue tumors based on physical examination alone. This presentation could easily lead to a misdiagnosis, delaying appropriate treatment. The differential diagnosis in such cases is broad, including other benign conditions such as epidermoid cysts, neurofibromas, and lipoblastomas, as well as malignant tumors like liposarcomas.Given the rarity of giant lipomas in the pediatric population, this case adds valuable information to the limited body of literature on the subject [17]. The histopathological analysis in this case confirmed the diagnosis of a benign lipoma, emphasizing the importance of tissue biopsy in cases where the clinical presentation is ambiguous. The biopsy ruled out malignancy, which is crucial given the potential for large, atypical lipomas to be mistaken for liposarcomas, a malignant counterpart with a different prognosis and treatment strategy [18].The standard management approach for giant lipomas typically involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging, and surgical intervention. The initial assessment includes a thorough physical examination, during which the characteristics of the mass—such as size, consistency, mobility, and tenderness—are noted. Given the size and unusual location of the mass in this case, imaging studies, particularly MRI, was crucial in delineating the mass's extent and its relationship to surrounding structures. MRI is the preferred imaging modality due to its superior soft tissue contrast, which helps in distinguishing lipomas from other soft tissue tumors. It also aids in surgical planning by defining the precise borders of the mass.Once imaging has confirmed the presence of a large, well-circumscribed mass consistent with a benign lipoma, the next step is often surgical excision. This is particularly true for giant lipomas due to the potential for physical discomfort, cosmetic concerns, and the rare but possible risk of malignant transformation [2]. Surgical excision involves the complete removal of the mass with a margin of normal tissue to ensure that no residual tumor is left behind, thereby minimizing the risk of recurrence. The excised tissue is then subjected to histopathological examination to confirm the diagnosis and rule out malignancy [19].In this case, a wide local excision was performed, which is the recommended approach for giant lipomas, especially those that are deeply embedded or located in anatomically complex regions like the gluteal area. The excision was successful, and the histopathological analysis confirmed the benign nature of the tumor, which is consistent with the standard management protocols described in the literature.When comparing our management approach to those described in other studies and case reports, it is evident that the approach of surgical excision following imaging is consistent across most cases of giant lipomas. The case emphasized the importance of MRI in preoperative planning and the successful outcome of wide local excision [20]. Similarly, a study by Mathew et al. (2010) reported on the management of a giant lipoma in the thigh, where wide excision was performed after confirming the diagnosis through MRI, with the postoperative outcome being favorable and no recurrence observed [21].One area of variation in the literature is the timing of surgical intervention. While most studies advocate for early excision, particularly in cases where the mass is symptomatic or cosmetically concerning, some reports suggest a more conservative approach in asymptomatic cases, particularly when the patient has significant comorbidities that may increase surgical risk. However, the general consensus remains that giant lipoma due to their size and the potential for complications, are best managed surgically [21].In terms of postoperative care, the focus is on monitoring for signs of recurrence, which, though rare, can occur if the excision was incomplete. Follow-up imaging may be warranted in some cases, particularly if there was any uncertainty about the completeness of the excision or if the histopathological findings were atypical. In our case, the patient was scheduled for regular follow-up visits to monitor for any signs of recurrence, which aligns with recommended practices in the management of giant lipomas [22].The delay in presentation observed in this case is a common issue in many low-resource settings and can significantly impact clinical outcomes. The reasons for delayed presentation are multifactorial, including socioeconomic factors, cultural beliefs, and limited access to healthcare facilities. The delay allowed the lipoma to grow to a size that caused significant physical and potentially psychological discomfort to the patient, necessitating a more complex surgical intervention. This case serves as a reminder of the importance of early detection and intervention in managing soft tissue tumors [23].Public health strategies that focus on improving awareness and access to healthcare could prevent similar cases from reaching such advanced stages. For example, community education programs that teach the importance of early medical evaluation of unusual growths could encourage earlier presentation and diagnosis. Additionally, healthcare systems in developing regions must be equipped to handle complex cases that may result from delayed presentation, ensuring that patients receive timely and appropriate care.4

Conclusion

In conclusion, the management of giant lipomas, particularly in pediatric populations, involves a multidisciplinary approach that includes thorough diagnostic evaluation, appropriate imaging, and surgical excision. This case illustrates the successful application of these principles in the management of a giant gluteal lipoma in a 14-year-old female. The comparison with other studies confirms that the approach taken in this case aligns well with the recommended standards of care, reinforcing the importance of early and accurate diagnosis, followed by definitive surgical management. This case also highlights the broader public health implications of delayed presentation and underscores the need for improved healthcare access and education in low-resource settings to prevent such cases from progressing to advanced stages.

PMC11417591.raw_case:
Uterine lymphangioleiomyomatosis in a premenopausal woman with tuberous sclerosis: A case report
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis is a rare disease characterized by abnormal smooth muscle cell growth. It primarily occurs in the lungs but can also rarely occur in other organs, in which case it is classified as extrapulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis. It often accompanies tuberous sclerosis complex. This report concerns a case of uterine lymphangioleiomyomatosis with spontaneous uterine rupture in a young woman with tuberous sclerosis complex. A 27-year-old nulligravida patient presented to the emergency room with vaginal bleeding. She had a history of clinical diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis complex and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Initially, abdominopelvic computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging suggested a hemorrhagic necrosis and rupture of degenerated uterine myoma. She underwent emergency exploratory laparotomy. The right side of her normal-sized uterus were ruptured without any specific mass. Active bleeding and hematoma from the ruptured uterus and partially ruptured right ovary were noted. The procedure included total hysterectomy and right salpingo-oophorectomy. Pathological analysis confirmed lymphangioleiomyomatosis in the uterine serosa and myometrium. Lymphangioleiomyomatosis mainly occurs in women of reproductive age and worsens with estrogen. Early diagnosis and careful follow-up are necessary due to the risk of worsening gynecological symptoms or even uterine rupture during pregnancy. This case enhances our understanding of extrapulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis and highlights the importance of comprehensive evaluation in complex clinical scenarios.

Highlights

•This report presents a case of a premenopausal woman with a history of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).•The patient was found to have spontaneous uterine rupture, requiring a total abdominal hysterectomy.•The pathological diagnosis was uterine lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM).•Uterine LAM is a rare manifestation of TSC, and only less than 30 cases of uterine LAM have been reported worldwide.•LAM occurs mainly in women of reproductive age and is worsened by estrogen, so early diagnosis and careful follow-up are necessary.1

Introduction

Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare disease characterized by abnormal smooth muscle cell growth, occurring mainly in women of reproductive age [1]. It is now considered a part of the family of perivascular epitheloid cell tumors (PEComa), which often infiltrate the smooth muscle of the blood vessels [2]. While most PEComas are benign, malignant forms can metastasize or recur. LAM primarily affects the lung parenchyma, leading to cystic destruction and respiratory failure [1]. However, it can also occur at extrapulmonary sites (EPLAM) along the axial lymphatic pathway in the abdominopelvic cavity, such as lymph nodes, retroperitoneum, and reproductive organs [3]. The clinical features of EPLAM vary based on organ involvement, from asymptomatic cases to abdominal pain or genital bleeding [[3], [4], [5]]. To date, fewer than 30 cases of uterine LAM have been reported worldwide [5].LAM occurs sporadically in 1 in 400,000 adult women but is found in up to 40 % of women with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) [3]. TSC is a disease-causing tumor in various organs due to mutation in the TSC genes [6]. Uterine LAM is a rare manifestation of TSC. This report concerns a case of uterine LAM with spontaneous rupture in a young woman with TSC.2

Case Presentation

A 27-year-old nulligravida woman presented to the emergency room with dizziness and vaginal bleeding. She had a history of clinical diagnosis of TSC, neurosurgical treatment for subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, LAM and multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia (MMPH) in lung, multiple bilateral renal angiomyolipomas (AMLs), hypomelanotic macule, and angiofibromas. No mutation was detected in the TSC2 gene. However, she had not visited the hospital for 3 years and was receiving no ongoing diagnostic evaluation or treatment.Her vital signs were stable, and she reported vague abdominal pain. However, her initial hemoglobin level was 6.0 g/dL, requiring transfusion of five packs of red blood cells. Abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated a hemorrhagic necrosis and rupture of degenerated uterine myoma into the endometrial and extrauterine cavity with massive hemoperitoneum (Fig. 1). Additionally, multiple AMLs up to 4 cm were noted in both kidneys. Compared to 3 years ago, no acute intracranial lesions, nor changes in pulmonary LAM and MMPH in brain CT and chest CT were observed, respectively.Surgery was performed in light of the stable vital signs and the findings on imaging. The patient had no sexual experience and had no wish to become pregnant. However, because she was a young woman of reproductive age, the possibility of hysterectomy was fully explained to her and her guardian before the surgery, and informed consent was obtained. She underwent an exploratory laparotomy under general anesthesia. More than 2 L of coagulated blood was removed. The right side of normal-sized uterus were ruptured without any specific mass. Bleeding and hematoma from the ruptured uterus and partially ruptured right ovary were noted. Small friable nodules were observed on the surface of the uterus and ovaries. The mass presumed to be a myoma rupture on imaging was actually a large hematoma with irregular margins and heterogenous echogenicity at the rupture site. A total hysterectomy and right salpingo-oophorectomy were performed. Upon cutting the uterus lengthwise, it was found to be full of hematoma inside.The pathological findings were as follows. The uterus measured 9 × 6 × 4 cm with hemorrhage and rupture of the myometrium in the right lateral wall of the uterine body. No diagnostic abnormalities in the right ovary and fallopian tube were noted. A 4.6 × 3.5 × 3 cm poorly demarcated infiltrative mass-like lesion was found in the uterine serosa, myometrium, and round ligament with mild cytologic atypia. Necrosis was not identified, and mitotic activity was <1/50 high-power fields (HPFs). Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining showed that the lesions were diffusely positive for human melanoma black-45 (HMB-45), a highly specific marker for LAM. An additional marker, smooth muscle α-actin (SMA), and estrogen receptor (ER) were also positive (Fig. 2).The patient's postoperative recovery was uneventful, and no unusual findings were noted during an outpatient visit 3 months after discharge. However, the patient strongly indicated that she did not want further diagnostic evaluation, treatment, or follow-up at the tertiary hospital due to the distance and cost, so no outpatient visits were done thereafter. The patient did, though, report no abnormalities in medical examinations and no unusual findings in a more recent gynecological examination at a local clinic.3

Discussion

Although the uterus is a common site of LAM involvement, uterine LAM is a very rare, with fewer than 30 histopathologically confirmed cases reported globally [5]. A previous literature review indicates that 40 % of uterine LAM are associated with TSC [7]. Therefore, uterine LAM should be considered in patients with a history of TSC presenting with vague gynecological symptoms.The clinical manifestations of uterine LAM can vary from being asymptomatic to causing symptoms such as dysmenorrhea, heavy menstrual bleeding, abnormal uterine bleeding or pelvic pain [[7], [8], [9]]. The definitive imaging features of uterine LAM remain elusive. Ultrasound reveals a heterogeneous echogenic mass within the uterus; however, it may also appear as a solid mass with high vascularity [10]. Even CT and MRI scans may present only nonspecific images: a diffuse, indistinct lesion lacking clear demarcation [5]. Similar to this case, Kim et al. described the radiological imaging findings of uterine LAM: multiple large, lobulated cystic uterine masses and a dilated endometrial cavity filled with fluid on contrast-enhanced CT [11]. On MRI, irregularly shaped uterine masses with high signal intensity were observed on the fat-suppressed T1-weighted images suggesting a hemorrhagic component. Due to its rarity and nonspecific symptoms and imaging studies, uterine LAM is often misdiagnosed as hemorrhagic or degenerative uterine leiomyomas, uterine malignancies, or adenomyosis [8,11]. In this case, too, it was initially misdiagnosed as a ruptured degenerated myoma. However, in similar future cases, uterine LAM should be considered when multiple cystic uterine masses are present in patients with TSC or pulmonary LAM.The diagnosis of uterine LAM can be confirmed through characteristic pathologic features and specific immunohistochemical stains. In particular, HMB-45 and SMA are recommended for accurate diagnosis, while the ER and progesterone receptor can aid in diagnosis [3]. Additionally, other markers such as vimentin and desmin can help differentiate LAM from other diseases [10]. LAM is considered one of the PEComa family: mesenchymal tumors with distinct IHC features, positive for both smooth muscle and melanocytic markers [2]. The cells of these tumors aggregate and infiltrate vascular muscles at multiple sites. PEComas range from benign to malignant, though the latter are rare. Malignant PEComa can be suspected when two or more of the following seven parameters are met: size >5 cm, high cellularity, high-grade nuclear atypia, mitotic activity >1/50 HPFs, necrosis, infiltrative margin, and vascular invasion [12]. This case met only the infiltrative margin criterion, suggesting a benign character.The etiology of LAM is related to genetic mutations in the tumor suppressor genes TSC1 and TSC2; these mutations are associated with pulmonary LAM and renal AML [2,13], but mutations in TSC genes can nevertheless often be found in cases of sporadic LAM [8]. TSC mutations cause overexpression of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex, forming benign tumors in various organs [[13], [14], [15]]. This patient underwent only TSC2 testing due to cost concerns, as TSC2 mutations are more common (70 %) than TSC1 mutations (20 %) and are associated with more severe phenotypes [16,17]. Although this patient did not have a mutation in the TSC2 gene, this does not rule out a diagnosis of TSC; this is because gene mutations are not found in up to 15 % of patients with TSC [13].Recently, estrogen has been considered another possible cause of LAM [3]. LAM mainly occurs in women of reproductive age, worsens with estrogen, and ER is confirmed in about half of cases. Therefore, hormonal changes during pregnancy may cause uterine LAM to enlarge and exacerbate symptoms. According to reported cases of PEComas during pregnancy, even previously small and asymptomatic uterine PEComas can grow rapidly, leading to uterine rupture by 30 weeks of gestation [18]. Another case report describes spontaneous hemoperitoneum resulting from a ruptured PEComa of the round ligaments at 34 weeks of gestation [19]. However, not all PEComas cause rupture during pregnancy, as some are disguised as retained placenta after a delivery [20]. Fertility preservation and management in patients with uterine LAM are important due to the risk of worsening gynecological symptoms or even uterine rupture during pregnancy. However, there is no established standard treatment for LAM or EPLAM. Medical treatments such as mTOR inhibitors or antiestrogen strategies are available; however, there is no firm data on their efficacy against the diseases [3]. Therefore, early diagnosis and careful follow-up are necessary.4

Conclusion

In conclusion, uterine LAM is a rare but important disease. It is generally considered a benign tumor that does not require further treatment [8,12]. However, as in this case, it can suddenly rupture in young women, with serious consequences, and occasionally present a malignant condition such as metastasis or sarcomatous transformation [9]. Therefore, when a patient with a history of TSC presents with abnormal uterine bleeding or abdominal pain, uterine LAM should be suspected and investigated. With few reported cases, this case enhances our understanding of uterine LAM and also highlights the need for further research due to its diverse presentation and diagnostic difficulties.

PMC11618002.raw_case:
Arteriovenous malformation associated with trophoblastic retention post-cesarean section: A case report and review


Introduction and importance

Uterine arteriovenous malformations are a rare but potentially life-threatening condition. They may be congenital or acquired and should be suspected in cases of severe or persistent uterine hemorrhage.

Case presentation

We present the clinical case of a 32-year-old woman who suffered from bleeding after a spontaneous miscarriage. Uterine arteriovenous malformation with trophoblastic retention was suspected on ultrasound and Doppler examination. Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the diagnosis, leading to embolization of both uterine arteries, followed by operative hysteroscopy to remove the retained tissue, with a favorable outcome.

Clinical discussion

Uterine arteriovenous malformation is rare, with fewer than 100 cases reported in the literature (1). It is a potentially fatal condition due to the heavy bleeding that patients may experience. Color Doppler ultrasound (US) is a non-invasive method for initially diagnosing this rare condition, which can be confirmed by diagnostic angiography. A conservative approach or embolization is the preferred treatment to avoid hysterectomy in patients of childbearing age.

Conclusions

This case report emphasizes the use of ultrasound and MRI to diagnose a uterine AVM in a patient of childbearing age who presented with post-partum retention of products. It also showcases our experience with embolization in this patient, which allowed her to preserve her fertility.

Highlights

•Uterine AVM is rare entities in gynecology, but they represent a potentially life-threatening disorder.•Ultrasound with Doppler can raise suspicion for the diagnosis, while MRI clarifies any uncertainties.•Embolization has become the preferred treatment, replacing hysterectomy.1

Introduction

Uterine arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a rare condition, with fewer than 100 cases documented in the literature [1]. It represents a major potential risk, as patients may be exposed to severe hemorrhage [2]. Color Doppler ultrasound (US) is an effective non-invasive method for the initial diagnosis of this pathology, which can be confirmed by diagnostic angiography. A conservative approach or embolization is a preferable treatment to avoid hysterectomy in patients of childbearing age [3]. This case report highlights our experience with a patient suffering from this rare gynecological pathology in our institution. This case was presented in accordance with the updated consensus Surgical Case Report (SCARE) guidelines [4].2

Case report

A 32-year-old G2P1 patient with no notable pathological antecedents, who underwent a cesarean section at term three years ago due to acute fetal distress, was admitted to our institution because of persistent low-grade metrorrhagia following a spontaneous miscarriage two months previously. She had initially been under observation for this bleeding, with a plasma beta HCG level measured at 13,500. The bleeding was considered to be due to trophoblastic retention, which led to her referral to our department for further treatment.Upon physical examination, the patient presented in good general condition, apyretic and hemodynamically stable, with no signs of anemia. A gynecological examination revealed a healthy cervix, with no vaginal lesions or active bleeding of endo-uterine origin.The plasma HCG assay was positive at 7100, slightly down on the previous test, with a hemoglobin level 12,1.Ultrasound combined with Doppler showed an anteverted and anteflexed uterus of normal morphology, measuring 50 (width) × 96 (height) × 44 (thickness) mm. The endometrium was thin and regular, with a heterogeneous image richly vascularised at the anterior isthmus over the cesarean scar, measuring 62 mm wide, 56 mm high, and 29 mm thick. Dilated vessels were observed, with veins showing velocities over 50 cm/s and low-resistance arteries with peaks over 100 cm/s (Fig. 1).A diagnosis of high-flow vascular malformations associated with trophoblastic retention on the isthmic cesarean scar was suspected. A pelvic Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) was then performed, confirming the presence of a retention measuring 30 mm associated with an AVM.Following a multidisciplinary consultation meeting, endovascular management was recommended, including embolization before evacuation of the retention by operative hysteroscopy.A right femoral arterial puncture was performed under local anesthetic with xylocaine and Risordan, followed by catheterization of the left uterine artery using a 5 French 135 cm BERN catheter. Arteriography revealed a large uterine arteriovenous formation, which was embolised with large (3/4) fragments of CURASPON, followed by a torpedo. The operation progressed favorably (Fig. 2).The patient underwent an operative hysteroscopy the same day to resect the trophoblastic retention. The operation revealed dehiscence of the anterior cesarean scar, with a retention of 3 to 4 cm long, partially necrotic and embedded in the scar. The operation was carried out without complications. Histopathological examination of the tissue revealed necrotic chorionic villi, confirming the diagnosis of an aborted pregnancy.The patient was followed up two weeks after the operation, reporting no bleeding, a negative beta HCG level, and an ultrasound showing regression of the AVM. At the 6-month check-up, she reported regular menstrual cycles with no abnormal uterine bleeding.3

Discussion

We present a rare case of acquired uterine AVM associated with trophoblastic retention, discovered after a miscarriage. The importance of this observation lies in the rarity of the cases reported and the originality of our diagnostic and therapeutic approach.Uterine AVM are rare entities in gynecology, but they represent a potentially life-threatening disorder, as patients may experience profuse metrorrhagia leading to hemodynamic instability. It is crucial to consider this differential diagnosis in women of childbearing age presenting with unexplained vaginal bleeding, as well as in post-menopausal women when an ultrasound scan reveals anechogenic structures [5]. Occasionally, these malformations may become apparent during exploration for pelvic pain, dyspareunia, or anemia [5].Uterine AVMs can be congenital or acquired [6]. Congenital AVMs are thought to arise from disruptions in embryological vascular development, leading to abnormal differentiation of capillaries and atypical connections between arteries and veins. These congenital forms may feature multiple vascular connections and can invade adjacent structures [7].Acquired AVMs are more prevalent and typically develop after uterine trauma, such as curettage, cesarean section, or pelvic surgery. The formation of abnormal connections between arteries and veins often occurs during the healing process, usually involving a single artery merging with a single vein. Additionally, acquired AVMs can be associated with infections, retained products of conception, gestational trophoblastic disease, and gynecological tumors [8].In cases of post-partum metrorrhagia, whether spontaneous or induced, the primary diagnosis to consider is often the retention, which may quickly necessitate uterine aspiration or curettage. However, in the presence of an AVM, this procedure can exacerbate the hemorrhage and pose a significant risk to the patient's life. Therefore, it is essential to highlight the importance of Doppler ultrasound in evaluating any instance of metrorrhagia to ensure that the possibility of an acquired AVM is not overlooked [9].Ultrasound, valued for its rapid, easy-to-perform, cost-effective, and non-invasive nature, has become the preferred technique for diagnosing arteriovenous AVMs. On greyscale ultrasound, uterine AVMs typically present as non-specific heterogeneous spaces within the myometrium, along with multiple cystic lesions and tubular anechoic areas. Common findings on color Doppler imaging include hypervascularization of the lesion, turbulent flow, and numerous tortuous feeding vessels, which may sometimes cause aliasing artifacts [10]. Spectral Doppler ultrasound reveals low values for both the resistance and pulsatility index, accompanied by high peak systolic velocity (PSV) flow. In normal myometrium, the PSV ranges from 9 to 44 cm/s, with a resistance index between 0.6 and 0.8, whereas in uterine AVMs, systolic and diastolic velocities can be 4 to 6 times higher [10].Studies have shown that PSV can be useful in distinguishing between safe and potentially dangerous AVMs [3]. A PSV of 0.83 m/s or greater is associated with malformations considered at risk, requiring immediate embolization. PSV values between 0.39 and 0.83 generally indicate a malformation of lesser concern, while values below 0.39 m/s are considered safe [3].Ultrasound is utilized to evaluate the effectiveness of embolization 24 hours post-procedure and to identify patients who may require repeat embolization. Additionally, it aids in differentiating between intrauterine retention, polyps, and endometrial hypertrophy [3].Digital subtraction angiography is considered the gold standard for diagnosing uterine AVM. This method demonstrates bilateral uterine artery hypertrophy and a hypertrophic, tortuous arterial mass with large feeding vessels. It confirms the diagnosis and identifies the main feeder vessels, thus guiding embolization [11].MRI is an effective method for diagnosing AVMs. When performed with a gadolinium-based contrast agent, MRI reveals predominantly arterial hypervascular flow and allows detailed assessment of vascular supply and drainage. Typical features of AVMs on MRI include a large uterus with a focal mass, junctional zone abnormalities, multiple areas of signal in the myometrium, intense enhancement on post-contrast images, and prominent parametrial vessels; however, disadvantages include high cost and limited availability in some regions [11].Three-dimensional tomography aims to determine the extent of the damage, exclude an ectopic lesion, distinguish congenital uterine AVMs from acquired ones, and identify the feeding vessels or uterine arteries [12].Computed tomography (CT) angiography can be used in patients who are unstable or have contraindications to MRI [13]. Although hysteroscopy can diagnose AVMs, its overall effectiveness is fairly limited [14].The strategy for treatment is primarily guided by the patient's hemodynamic status, the severity of the bleeding, age, desire for future fertility, potential for recurrence, and available treatment options.Initial management aims to stabilize the patient's hemodynamic status and stop any bleeding. Traditionally, hysterectomy was the preferred treatment, but the patient's desire to become pregnant is an essential consideration. Today, uterine embolization is the treatment of choice [15]. It has three main advantages: first, it allows for confirmation of the pre-treatment diagnosis during the arteriographic phase; second, it provides a quick and minimally invasive procedure; and third, it helps preserve the patient's obstetric prognosis. Selective embolization may be unilateral or bilateral, depending on the location of the feeding arteries. Various agents, such as coils, gelatin sponges, polyvinyl alcohol, detachable balloons, and isobutyl-2-cyanoacrylate, have been used for uterine artery embolization. The choice of agent depends on the size of the vessel to be embolized and whether temporary or permanent occlusion is required [16].Potential side effects may include mild fever, pain, infection, temporary lameness in the buttocks and lower limbs, peeling of the perineal skin, utero-vaginal and recto-vesico-vaginal fistulas, and bladder necrosis [17]. However, the risk of complications is extremely rare and significantly minimized when the procedure is conducted by a specialist in interventional radiology.It is important to note that embolization does not affect the menstrual cycle or pregnancy [17].Hysterectomy remains the treatment of choice for postmenopausal women with AVMs, for women who do not wish to preserve their fertility, as an emergency procedure in life-threatening conditions, or if transcatheter embolization fails [18]. Other surgical methods rarely used include hysteroscopic coagulation, laparoscopic coagulation, surgical ablation, and uterine artery ligation.In stable patients that can be closely monitored, a long-term conservative approach may be appropriate. Timmerman et al. reported that six out of ten cases of uterine AVMs resolved spontaneously, and oral contraception and methylergonovine maleate, administered first intramuscularly and then orally, are associated with regression of lesions [6].4

Conclusion

Arteriovenous malformations are rare and should be considered in cases of persistent bleeding in women of childbearing age with a history of spontaneous abortion, whether or not they have undergone uterine curettage. This awareness can help avoid interventions that may exacerbate the condition and facilitate timely, appropriate management. Ultrasound with Doppler can raise suspicion for the diagnosis, while MRI clarifies any uncertainties from ultrasound and offers a precise topographical diagnosis. Embolization has become the preferred treatment, replacing hysterectomy, which was previously the standard approach.

Abbreviations


AVMarteriovenous malformation


Consent

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying images. A copy of the written consent is available for review by the Editor-in-Chief of this journal.

Ethical approval

It is not necessary to obtain specific ethical approval from the Mohamed V Military Hospital for this situation. The case report does not contain any personal information.

All authors have read and approved the final manuscript.
