PMC11525064.raw_case:
Primary intraosseous meningioma: a case of early symptomatic calvarial origin meningioma


Abstract

Primary intraosseous meningiomas are rare extradural tumors. They are typically slow-growing, painless, and asymptomatic until they cause a mass effect. We report a case of a calvarial primary intraosseous meningioma, which became symptomatic despite a very small size. A 67-year-old female with a history of precancerous breast tissue presented with right-sided stroke-like symptoms. Computed tomography showed right parietal convexity irregularity without hemorrhage or infarct. MRI indicated a right parietal calvarial signal abnormality and dural thickening, suggesting metastases or primary osseous neoplasm. A PET scan revealed heterogeneous uptake in the right parietal skull with no other abnormalities. Histology confirmed the diagnosis of primary intraosseous meningioma. Histopathological examination is crucial to avoid misdiagnosis and treatment planning, which may involve wide-margin skull resection, radiation, or both.

Introduction

Meningiomas are the most common central nervous system (CNS) tumors, accounting for about 30% of all cases [1, 2]. Primary extradural meningiomas (PEMs) are a rare subtype of meningiomas that account for less than 2% of all meningiomas [2, 3]. Primary Intraosseous meningioma (PIOM) is a subtype of extradural meningioma that arises in bones and accounts for two-thirds of all PEMs [4]. The incidence of PEMs is slightly higher in females [5, 6], with one peak in the second decade of life and the other between 50 and 70 years old [2, 6]. Here, we present a case of parietal intraosseous meningioma that, despite its very small size, manifested with stroke-like symptoms.

Case report

A 67-year-old female presented with transient right-sided stroke-like symptoms. The initial CT scan and MRI with and without contrast revealed a right parietal convexity heterogeneous enhancement of the calvarium with subjacent dural thickening, extending from the posterior frontal bone, concerning metastases or possibly primary osseous neoplasm. No hemorrhage or large vessel territory and no epidural mass were observed (Fig. 1). A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed heterogeneous mild to moderate abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake involving the right-sided parietal skull sclerotic lesion and no other site of abnormal uptake. She had a past medical history of right-sided breast atypical ductal hyperplasia, which was removed four years ago.She underwent a craniectomy and skull biopsy. Gross examination revealed tan-pink soft tissue and bone fragments, with the largest specimen measuring 1.5 × 0.6 × 0.3 cm. Microscopically, the tumor showed a syncytial growth pattern with meningothelial whorls. Tumor cells were focally positive for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), progesterone receptor (PR), and somatostatin receptor 2A(SSTR2A), with Ki67 < 1% (Fig. 2). During the subsequent surgery two months later, the tumor-involved skull and adherent dura were removed through a wide excision, and a 10 × 10 cm cranioplasty was performed.Pathology showed a sheet-like growth pattern with rare prominent nucleoli, a mitotic count of less than 2 per 10 high-power fields, Ki-67 15%–20%, and a focal rhabdoid morphology Fig. 3). Molecular testing was negative for CDKN2A homozygous deletions and Telomerase Reverse Transcriptase (TERT) promoter mutations. The patient was stable after the surgery and the six-month follow-up with no recurrence or residual extra-axial lesions.

Discussion

The clinical presentation of PIOMs depends on their size and location [6, 7]. The most common presentation of calvarial-origin PIOM is a slow-growing asymptomatic mass that grows until it becomes large enough to cause a mass effect. Headaches are the second most frequently reported symptom [8]. The pathogenesis of PIOM is still unclear and controversial. Some authors suggest that its origin is related to the intracranial suture line, where a portion of the dura mater or arachnoid cap cells become trapped in the suture line due to trauma, embryonic development, or head molding at birth [2].Microscopically, the tumor is most often WHO grade 1 [5, 9] and exhibits a syncytial growth pattern with meningothelial whorls and is positive for EMA, PR, and SSTR2A [10]. These tumors can also be subclassified based on their anatomical location into convexity and skull base lesions [4]. The most common locations are the orbital cavity and frontoparietal area, most commonly in the frontal bone (29.1%) [11]. The optimal treatment is surgical excision, with a reported recurrence rate of 12.6% to 22% postsurgery [12]. The skull base meningiomas have a higher recurrence rate due to the challenges in achieving complete resection in these areas [12]. However, Ueno et al. reported a case of transitional meningioma (WHO grade I) convexity PIOM that recurred seven years after the surgery [2]. Chen et al. reported even histologically benign but unresectable PIOMs may exhibit malignant changes over time [3]. Several recent studies highlight the significance of molecular features in assessing the risk of recurrence [13]. The 2021 WHO CNS5 classifies meningiomas into three grades using both histopathology and molecular features. Grade 1 tumors with mutations like pTERT or CDKN2A/B deletion are upgraded to grade 3, indicating more aggressive behavior and higher recurrence risk. This shift highlights the importance of molecular profiling for accurate tumor grading and treatment planning [2, 13]. In our case, molecular testing for CDKN2A deletions and TERT mutations was negative. While reassuring, these results still underscore the need for preventive management and emphasize the role of molecular testing in personalized care and treatment decisions.Tumor location is also associated with specific underlying mutations. Convexity and most spinal meningiomas frequently exhibit 22q deletions and NF2 mutations. In contrast, skull base meningiomas are often characterized by mutations in AKT1, TRAF7, SMO, and/or PIK3CA [9, 13]. PIOMs can also be subclassified into osteoblastic, osteolytic, or mixed types and mimic a wide range of benign or malignant lesions, either metastatic or primary bone tumors [2, 10, 14]. The osteolytic subtype is less frequent in PIOMs, with reported rates ranging from rare to 35% [2]. Hyperostosis is more common in low-grade meningiomas. In contrast, a mixed hyperostotic/lytic pattern is typically associated with higher grade meningiomas [15]. Some of the differential diagnoses include osteosarcoma, eosinophilic granuloma, Paget disease, osteoblastic skull metastasis, osteoma, fibrous dysplasia, en plaque meningioma, plasmacytoma, giant cell tumor, hemangioma, epidermoid cyst, osteogenic sarcoma, aneurysmal bone cyst, fibrous dysplasia, or infection [16]. Imaging studies, clinical presentations, and histological evaluations are essential for differential diagnosis [10]. Each of these conditions may show bone involvement or destruction; however, they vary in their underlying mechanisms and clinical progression. The diagnosis can be challenging and histologically misdiagnosed. Immunohistochemistry is very useful in distinguishing PIM from a primary or secondary bone tumor [16]. Blood tests, such as alkaline phosphatase levels, can assist rule out important differential diagnoses such as Paget’s disease of the bone [5]. The combination of MRI and CT scans helps the diagnosis of ICM in most cases [17].Our case was diagnosed as meningothelial meningioma, WHO grade 1, and was reported as a heterogeneous, well-defined enhancement in MRI. The dura-tail sign, characterized by thickening of the dura adjacent to an intracranial pathology on MRI, is a useful marker in diagnosing meningiomas. It is typically associated with convexity meningiomas but can also be present in PEMs and is not indicative of dural origin, although PEMs can invade the dura and make a dural tail sign [2, 4, 11]. In our case, there was no sign of a dural tail, which supported the extradural origin and differentiated it from typical convexity meningioma extending outside the dura. Histopathological studies report that the rate of dural infiltration in PIOMs ranges from 26% to 87.5%, while radiographic studies indicate a range of 60.0%–68.8%. These findings suggest that PIOMs have a significant propensity to infiltrate the dura [2]. To prevent future recurrence or progression to a malignant grade, management is often wide excision and long-term follow-up [2, 7]. Most calvarial meningiomas are benign and slow-growing, but compared with intracranial meningiomas, PEMs are more prone to develop malignant changes [4]. The treatment of choice in symptomatic cases is extensive surgical excision. Total resection of the dura at the craniotomy site should be considered, as PEMs and PIOMs could recur even if intraoperative findings do not show any dural invasion. Adjuvant therapy is recommended for unresectable or partially resectable symptomatic tumors or those with malignant or atypical histology. Treatment options may include radiation therapy such as external beam or Gamma Knife surgery, as well as chemotherapy and bisphosphonate therapy [2, 14].Recurrence has been reported in atypical or malignant intraosseous meningioma within two years and in histologically benign tumors within 10 years after the resection [4, 14]. Limited long-term follow-up information is available for PIM due to their uncommon nature. However, studies indicate that the recurrence rates for benign meningiomas originating from the calvarium vary between 12.6% and 22% [12]. Therefore, regular imaging surveillance and close monitoring of patients are crucial to evaluate the extent of resection, early detection of recurrence or malignant progression, and timely intervention [10]. In cases of suspected meningiomas or those classified as WHO grade 1, annual MRI scans are recommended for 5 years. Following this period, the frequency of the scans may be increased to every 2 years [17] and continued monitoring for any neurological changes or tumor regrowth is recommended.PIOM diagnosis can be challenging due to its rarity and asymptomatic progression. Imaging studies are essential in identifying PIOMs; however, histopathology remains the gold standard for confirming the diagnosis. Due to the rarity of these tumors, it is crucial to have a high suspicion in the differential diagnosis. Timely and accurate diagnoses can significantly improve treatment outcomes, highlighting the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration between radiologists, pathologists, and neurosurgeons in developing effective treatment plans for individual patient needs. Careful long-term follow-up is recommended regardless of the pathological findings or degree of gross removal.

PMC11585286.raw_case:
Moderately Advanced Local Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma With Significant Tumor Burden
Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a prevalent malignancy with a steadily increasing incidence. Associated risk factors range from tobacco use to the presence of human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Despite advances in therapeutic options, there have been minimal improvements in the survival rate and percentage of morbidity and mortality. Here, we report the case of a 55-year-old male who presented with failure to thrive secondary to moderately advanced local OSCC, staged T4a N0 M0, and discuss specific considerations regarding prognosis and delayed diagnosis.

Introduction

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the eighth leading cause of cancer worldwide and is also the most common malignancy of the head and neck [1]. Annually, about 300,000 cases of oral and oropharyngeal cancer are diagnosed worldwide [2]. Common development sites include the tongue, lips, and floor of the mouth. Risk factors include tobacco use, alcohol consumption, increasing age, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and human papillomavirus (HPV). Both tobacco use and alcohol consumption are associated with a six-fold increased risk of developing oral cancer. The combination of tobacco and alcohol use poses a fifteen-fold increased risk of oral cancer [2].Staging for OSCC is classically performed using the TNM staging system [3]. Prognosis is best when OSCC is diagnosed early, is well-differentiated, and has not yet metastasized. While certain variables, including patient age, comorbidities, tumor size and location, nodal status, oncogene expression, and proliferation markers have been assessed as independent prognostic markers for oral cancer, the most important prognostic factor remains the stage at the time of diagnosis [4]. Delayed diagnosis leads to a delay in treatment and disease progression, which can potentially progress to regional and distant metastasis. Despite the risks associated with delayed diagnosis, most OSCC cases are diagnosed at later stages of the disease. The mortality rate has remained mostly unchanged for decades with an estimated 50% 5-year survival rate, even with advances in surgery and radiotherapy [2]. A delay in diagnosis could be one large contributing factor to the stagnant mortality rate. This case report discusses the workup of a patient with moderately advanced OSCC who experienced a delay in diagnosis.

Case presentation

A 55-year-old Hispanic male with a known history of T4aN0M0 p16 negative OSCC, with a large tumor invading the tongue, floor of the mouth, mandible, and skin of the face presented to the emergency department with complaints of inability to tolerate oral intake. The patient stated that he had been experiencing new-onset dysphagia with solid foods for approximately two months and difficulty tolerating liquids for approximately three weeks. He noted that more recently when he attempted to consume liquids, approximately half of his oral intake would come out of a pre-existing facial lesion. The patient had no significant past medical or surgical history. Social history was significant for a 15-pack-year history and alcohol intake of an estimated 16 beers per week.The patient was diagnosed with p16 negative invasive moderately to poorly differentiated OSCC just one month before the time of presentation after undergoing an anterior lower gingival buccal sulcus biopsy secondary to concerns for an oral mass and facial swelling. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the soft tissue of the neck at the time of diagnosis demonstrated a large heterogeneous fluid collection extending from the anterior soft tissues of the chin into the oral cavity (Figure 1). Before undergoing the diagnostic biopsy, the patient had previously been seen in the emergency department secondary to concerns for facial swelling but was discharged home on antibiotics as the swelling was presumed to be infectious.A repeat CT of the soft tissue of the neck was performed during this admission and demonstrated again a large ulcerated, lobulated, peripherally enhancing, and nodular mass involving the mandibular anterior buccal soft tissues extending to the gingival surface and floor of the mouth, concerning malignancy (Figure 2). CT of the chest demonstrated no evidence of acute or metastatic process. On extraoral examination, a large orocutaneous fistula was visualized (Figure 3). Erosion of the anterior mandible with overlying poor dentition and foul drainage was also noted during the inspection. The patient’s tongue was firm, fixed, and restricted in movement on command, leading to dysarthria. The patient endorsed significant pain, which he localized to the site of the orocutaneous fistula. Given concerns about inadequate oral intake and failure to thrive, the patient was ultimately admitted. Due to the patient’s lack of oral intake, enteral nutrition was deemed necessary. General surgery was consulted for percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube placement; however, the patient instead underwent fluoroscopically guided percutaneous gastrostomy tube placement with interventional radiology to minimize the risk of seeding the known carcinoma during the procedure. Following the establishment of enteral nutrition, the patient was monitored and medically optimized until he was transferred to a dedicated cancer center for planned operative intervention.Upon transfer, the patient ultimately underwent composite resection of the oral cavity with bilateral modified radical neck dissections, tracheostomy, anterior glossectomy, osteotomy of the neo-mandible and mandibular reconstruction with transosteal plate, left pectoralis major flap with adjacent tissue transfer and Integra placement, right osteocutaneous fibular free flap with Integra placement, and right anterolateral thigh free flap with adjacent tissue transfer. Postoperative imaging demonstrated nonspecific swelling of the anterior soft tissues of the neck status post complex jaw reconstruction with myocutaneous free flap reconstruction without evidence of recurrence of malignancy (Figure 4). The patient tolerated the procedure well and was ultimately discharged with instructions to follow up with oncology regarding future chemoradiation needs.

Discussion

Oral cancer accounts for approximately 2-4% of all cancer cases worldwide, with OSCC representing more than 90% of all oral neoplasms [2]. The primary sites include the buccal mucosa, upper and lower gingiva, hard palate, tongue, floor of the mouth, and retromolar trigone [4]. Associated risk factors include tobacco and alcohol use, premalignant lesions, increasing age, HIV, and HPV. Survival rates for oral cancer are poor, estimated to be around 50% overall, and no significant improvements have been made in recent decades despite advances in the available therapeutic interventions [5]. Even with the presence of numerous independent prognostic markers for oral cancer, including patient age, tumor location and size, and oncogene expression, the stage of diagnosis remains the most important prognostic factor [4]. Detection at an early stage is the single most effective way to reduce morbidity and mortality, and improve patient quality of life [5].While prognosis is typically the best when OSCC is diagnosed early, most cases continue to be diagnosed at later stages. Approximately 60% of cases are identified in advanced stages, defined as stages III or IV [4]. Part of the delay in diagnosis is secondary to delayed reporting of symptoms as the initial symptoms experienced by patients tend to be general, including pain, swelling, and other similar complaints of the jaw. Emphasis on awareness and appropriate education of patients is crucial. Providers especially need to be educating patients who have significant risk factors, such as alcohol and tobacco use.Another aspect to consider in the delay in diagnosis is the role of healthcare providers and the necessity of an appropriate diagnostic workup. In the case report presented above, the patient was previously seen in the emergency department secondary to concerns for facial swelling but was discharged home on antibiotics and the diagnosis was missed. The lack of an appropriate diagnostic workup poses a direct challenge in adequate diagnostic timing and can complicate the future treatment plan. Again, education is crucial to raise awareness for early diagnosis and better prognosis of OSCC. To aid in earlier diagnosis, healthcare providers should be knowledgeable about the early signs of oral carcinoma and should perform oral cancer screening examinations of high-risk individuals, along with educating the general public to raise awareness.While educational interventions should be provided to the general public, efforts regarding knowledge of disease presentation should be particularly focused on those high-risk patient groups and healthcare professionals. With increased awareness and education regarding the signs and symptoms of OSCC, there is a possibility of earlier diagnosis, improved treatment outcomes, and potentially, higher survival rates.

Conclusions

In the case described above, the patient initially presented with facial swelling and eventually developed a large orocutaneous fistula before being diagnosed with moderately advanced local OSCC. The patient ultimately underwent complex jaw reconstruction with myocutaneous free flap and is currently working with oncology regarding future chemoradiation needs. Given the correlation of early disease identification with both reduced morbidity and improved patient quality of life, early diagnosis is crucial. Future research efforts should be conducted with an emphasis on improving both prevention and early detection of OSCC.

PMC11584938.raw_case:
Ureaplasma urealyticum pyelonephritis associated with renal, perinephric, retroperitoneal, and bladder abscesses in a hypogammaglobinemic adult patient presenting with gross hematuria and marked thrombocytosis
Ureaplasma urealyticum is an opportunistic bacterium that is often identified in asymptomatic, healthy individuals from colonization of the genitourinary tract. However, in immunocompromised patients with hypogammaglobulinemia, Ureaplasma has been reported to cause a wide range of infections, most commonly urethritis and cystitis. The absence of a bacterial cell wall prevents Ureaplasma from being cultured using routine bacteriologic media and makes it resistant to commonly prescribed antibiotics. As a result, delayed or missed diagnosis can occur with patients initially receiving inadequate medical management. The use of broad-range bacterial polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification to detect bacterial ribonucleic acid is often required to make the diagnosis in suspected cases. We present a rare case of Ureaplasma urealyticum causing histopathologically-confirmed unilateral pyelonephritis with associated renal, perinephric, retroperitoneal, and bladder abscesses in a hypogammaglobinemic adult patient. We performed a literature review for cases of Ureaplasma urealyticum causing upper urinary tract infections and nephric-perinephric abscesses and found that these are extremely rare manifestations.

Introduction

Ureaplasma urealyticum, a bacterium belonging to the family Mycoplasmataceae, is commonly found in the genitourinary tracts of sexually active, healthy individuals, of which the majority are asymptomatic with genitourinary colonization [1]. However, it has previously been proposed that Ureaplasma may have enhanced virulence in immunocompromised individuals with hypogammaglobulinemia, with a limited number of case reports identifying Ureaplasma as the causative agent for urethritis, cystitis, polyarthritis, osteomyelitis, and pneumonia in patients with hypogammaglobulinemia [2], [3], [4], [5]. Primary hypogammaglobulinemia from a genetic condition like common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) has been associated with disseminated Ureaplasma infection [6], [7], [8]. With the recent expanded use of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies, there has been an increased incidence of secondary hypogammaglobulinemia [9]. The overwhelming majority of reported Ureaplasma-related urinary tract infections in the literature involve the lower urinary tract (urethritis or cystitis) [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18]. Currently, only a few case reports have identified Ureaplasma as the causative agent in immunocompromised adult patients with upper urinary tract infections (ureteritis or pyelonephritis) [19], [20], [21], [22]. We present a rare case of Ureaplasma urealyticum causing histopathologically-confirmed unilateral pyelonephritis with associated renal, perinephric, retroperitoneal, and bladder abscesses in an immunocompromised adult patient with hypogammaglobulinemia.

Case presentation

A 29-year-old Caucasian female with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis for which receiving anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody therapy (initially rituximab and more recently ocrelizumab) over the past four years every 6 months, presented to the hospital with chronic gross hematuria and multiple non-specific symptoms including fatigue, weakness, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, and lightheadedness. Other past medical history included diabetes mellitus type 1 which was well-controlled on an insulin pump, hypothyroidism, and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection without respiratory symptoms diagnosed ten days prior to presentation. She reported a history of chronic gross hematuria of unclear etiology that began nine months prior to presentation for which she was previously seen by an outside urologist and was diagnosed with interstitial cystitis. Physical exam at time of presentation revealed blood pressure 95/61 mmHg, heart rate 116 beats per minute, temperature 37.1 °C, and mild crackles of the posterior lung bases bilaterally. Laboratory workup (Table 1) demonstrated a white blood cell (WBC) count of 18,700 WBCs/mcL with 83 % neutrophils, platelet count of 842,000 platelets/mcL, hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL, serum creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL (eGFR of 87 mL/min/BSA per CKD-EPI), serum Cystatin C of 1.10 mg/L (eGFR of 72 mL/min/BSA per CKD-EPI), serum albumin of 3.3 g/dL, and hemoglobin A1c of 6.2 %. Urinalysis with microscopy obtained on admission revealed > 182 WBC/hpf, 151 RBC/hpf, WBC clumps present, large leukocyte esterase, negative nitrite, negative glucose. Urine culture and blood cultures (bacterial and fungal) obtained prior to administration of any antimicrobial agents were no growth. Urine pregnancy test was negative. Chest x-ray showed ground-glass changes of the mid and lower interstitial lung spaces. Given her gross hematuria, a CT urogram was obtained which revealed multifocal left upper pole and interpolar renal pyelonephritis with an associated large 9.5 cm left nephric-perinephric abscess extending into the left retroperitoneum, an anterior lateral 2.5 cm intraparenchymal left renal abscess, cystitis and left ureteritis, and moderate bilateral hydroureteronephrosis (left greater than right). Subsequent MRI of the pelvis also showed findings of an anterior-superior bladder abscess. As she met criteria for sepsis with pyelonephritis and associated renal, perinephric, retroperitoneal, and bladder abscesses, she was started on broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage, initially with piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy but later broadened to include combination of a carbapenem, vancomycin, and amphotericin B after she developed high-grade sustained fever and persistent leukocytosis. She underwent cystoscopy by urology with left ureteral stent placement given findings of hydronephrosis on CT urogram. She underwent aspiration with drain placement by interventional radiology of her left perinephric-retroperitoneal abscess, left superior-anterior renal abscess, and anterior-superior bladder abscess, all of which had purulent output. Despite having purulent fluid from all these drainage sites, gram stains were negative and cultures (bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal) all remained no growth with exception of Candida glabrata from initial drainage of the anterior-superior bladder abscess. Testing for Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, human immunodeficiency virus, Coccidioides, Cryptococcus, Blastomyces, and Histoplasma were all negative. Cytology of all sites was unremarkable. Given her severe and persistent thrombocytosis (reaching up to 1028,000 platelets/mcL) with associated leukocytosis (reaching up to 26,900 WBCs/mcL) and anemia (requiring transfusion of 2 units packed red blood cells) over the course of her hospitalization, hematology was consulted. After extensive workup to evaluate for possible reactive and autonomous causes (Table 1), the patient’s severe thrombocytosis and leukocytosis was contributed to reactive process from her underlying infection. Testing for serum immunoglobulins (Ig) was performed given her use of ocrelizumab which revealed hypogammaglobulinemia with low IgG of 445 mg/dL (normal 767–1590), low IgM of 23 mg/dL (normal 37–286), and normal IgA of 133 mg/dL (normal 61–356). Outside records revealed that that patient had normal serum immunoglobulins (IgG and IgM) before being started on ocrelizumab. During her hospitalization, she received intravenous immunoglobulin 25 g x2 doses separated 3 days apart with subsequent normalization of her serum IgG to 1050 mg/dL. As she remained febrile with persistent leukocytosis and no clinical improvement despite aspiration of abscesses and broad-spectrum antibacterial and antifungal therapy, a left native renal biopsy was obtained. Histopathology revealed findings confirming pyelonephritis with marked suppurative inflammation (Fig. 1A & 1B). Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) fungal stain (Fig. 1C) and acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain (Fig. 1D) of the renal biopsy were both negative. Renal histopathology was not suggestive of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, inflammatory pseudotumor, malacoplakia, eosinophilic nephritis, or malignancy. Given persistent lack of any clinical improvement, patient ultimately underwent left-sided radical open nephrectomy. Broad-range bacterial PCR sequencing from the initial renal biopsy eventually returned positive for Ureaplasma urealyticum. Histopathology from the patient’s nephrectomy showed findings of pyelonephritis with organizing abscess and numerous cortical microabscesses (Fig. 2A & 2B). Repeat broad-range bacterial PCR sequencing from nephrectomy tissue was also positive for Ureaplasma urealyticum. Her antimicrobial regimen was subsequently adjusted to include doxycycline which she received 100 mg twice per day for a total of 7 days post-nephrectomy for targeted therapy of Ureaplasma. Following her left-sided radical nephrectomy and initiation of doxycycline therapy for coverage of Ureaplasma, she had resolution of her fevers, tachycardia, and leukocytosis, in addition to marked improvement of her thrombocytosis.

Discussion

Ureaplasma was first described in 1954 by Shepard after culturing this genus of bacteria from the urethras of men with non-gonococcal urethritis [23]. Ureaplasma species are unique in that they lack a bacterial cell wall. Consequently, Ureaplasma bacteria are osmotically fragile, cannot be visualized by routine gram staining, require a special culture medium containing sterols for growth, and are resistant to commonly prescribed antibiotics that target the bacterial cell wall [23], [24]. It is estimated that Ureaplasma is found on the mucosal surfaces of the genital tract (vagina and cervix) from colonization in 40–80 % of asymptomatic adult women [23], [25]. Immunocompromised individuals with hypogammaglobulinemia have an increased risk of this opportunistic pathogen causing genitourinary and extragenital infections [22]. As Ureaplasma species are resistant to beta lactams, sulfonamides, aminoglycosides, and clindamycin, antibiotic treatment requires the use of tetracyclines, macrolides, or fluoroquinolones.Currently, Ureaplasma is not medically recognized as a potential causative bacterium for pyelonephritis and nephric-perinephric abscesses. This lack of recognition is partly due to the previously mentioned challenges faced with making the diagnosis and the few reported human cases described in medical literature. Previous research by Pickering showed that a single reflux challenge of Ureaplasma urealyticum into rat kidneys resulted in histopathological changes consistent with Ureaplasma urealyticum-induced chronic pyelonephritis [26]. A thorough literature review revealed only 4 prior reported human cases of upper urinary tract infections from Ureaplasma, all of which involved immunocompromised female patients [19], [20], [21], [22]. Yazdani described an immunocompromised female with right pyelonephritis and perinephric abscess from Ureaplasma
[19]. Ngoo reported an immunocompromised female with multiple left renal and perinephric abscesses from Ureaplasma
[20]. Schwartz described an immunocompromised female with pyelonephritis from Ureaplasma
[21]. Jhaveri reported an immunocompromised female with bilateral nephric abscesses from Ureaplasma
[22]. Similar to our case, in all 4 of these case reports, there was no organism identified using standard microscopy, and cultures from all drained abscesses, blood, and urine samples using routine media were no growth. Also like our case, the diagnosis in three of these case reports (Yazdani, Ngoo, and Schwartz) required the use of broad-range bacterial PCR sequencing, whereas the fourth (Jhaveri) used “specialized urine culture techniques” to isolate the organism [19], [20], [21], [22].Our patient was immunocompromised based on her use of ocrelizumab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, for her multiple sclerosis which likely contributed to her hypogammaglobinemia. Most cases of infection related Ureaplasma have been associated with hypogammaglobinemia from the use of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies [22]. Chronic urethritis-cystitis has been previously associated with Ureaplasma infection in hypogammaglobulinemic patients [2]. Ureaplasma species have known IgA protease activity which has been proposed as a potential virulence factor given that IgA is the predominant immunoglobulin secreted by mucosal surfaces [23], [27], [28]. Additional research is needed to further understand the mechanism in which Ureaplasma as an opportunistic pathogen can result in genitourinary and extragenital infections in certain immunocompromised individuals. Future research should also explore why females appear to be more prone to developing localized and systemic infections over males.

Conclusion

We present a case of Ureaplasma urealyticum causing pyelonephritis with numerous associated genitourinary abscesses (nephric, perinephric, retroperitoneal, and bladder) as evidenced by renal histopathology and broad-range bacterial PCR sequencing. This case report highlights the importance of considering atypical organisms like Ureaplasma and Mycoplasma as causative infectious agents in hypogammaglobinemic patients with obvious signs of infection but negative bacterial and fungal cultures using routine media. This case report also highlights the utility of using broad-range bacterial PCR sequencing to detect and identify culture-negative bacterial infections. Medical providers should recognize Ureaplasma as a potential causative bacterium for pyelonephritis and genitourinary-associated abscesses in hypogammaglobinemic patients, especially given the recent expanded use of anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies.

Ethics

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and accompanying histopathology images. A copy of the written consent is available for review by the Editor-in-Chief of this journal on request.

Consent

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and accompanying histopathology images. A copy of the written consent is available for review by the Editor-in-Chief of this journal on request.

No funding was needed or received for the creation of this manuscript.

PMC11564058.raw_case:
Mixed connective tissue disease: A case of aggressive progression and multisystem involvement
Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is a rare autoimmune syndrome characterized by overlapping features of systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and polymyositis, first described by Sharp et al. in 1972. This case report discusses a 38-year-old female who presented with symptoms indicative of these overlapping conditions, including sclerodactyly, Raynaud's phenomenon, and muscle weakness, confirmed by laboratory findings and imaging. Despite aggressive treatment with immunosuppressive agents such as methotrexate, corticosteroids, and infliximab, the patient's condition progressively deteriorated, leading to severe complications, including interstitial lung disease and gastrointestinal involvement. Mixed connective tissue disease remains a complex and poorly understood condition with a range of clinical presentations and no distinct risk factors. The prognosis varies significantly, with some patients experiencing life-threatening complications while others may achieve complete remission. Diagnostic criteria, such as the Alarcon-Segovia criteria, and serological markers like anti-U1RNP antibodies, are critical in identifying and managing this rare and challenging condition.

Introduction

Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) is a disease syndrome with overlapping features of systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and polymyositis was first described by Sharp et al. in 1972. Hence, MCTD is sometimes described as an overlap disease. Patients typically present with nonspecific symptoms such as swollen digits, arthralgia, myalgia, muscle weakness, acid reflux or dysphagia, Raynaud's phenomenon, shortness of breath when active, and general fatigue. As the symptoms progress, one or more of the 3 illnesses are predominant along with high anti-U1RNP antibody titers. Mixed connective tissue disorder is unknown in its etiology, but being an autoimmune disease, it tends to run in families and affects women more than men. Due to the lack of causal associations and the range of presentation of this rare condition, it is difficult to diagnose [1].We describe a 38-year-old female with no significant family history of autoimmune diseases initially presented with symptoms that evolved into a complex overlap syndrome involving systemic sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and polymyositis. Despite various treatments, including NSAIDs, adalimumab, methotrexate, and corticosteroids, her condition progressively worsened, leading to multiple complications such as interstitial lung disease, gastrointestinal involvement, and sacroiliitis. Her treatment has been managed by a multidisciplinary team, but her prognosis remains guarded due to the severe and chronic nature of her autoimmune conditions, which continue to impact her quality of life significantly.

Case presentation

A 38-year-old female with no significant family history of autoimmune diseases. She initially presented with symptoms including fever, cough, headache, lower abdominal pain, heartburn and regurgitation. Despite an initial conservative approach involving symptomatic management with NSAIDs and antipyretics, her condition escalated, leading to further investigation. On physical examination, she exhibited skin thickening and tightening, particularly over the fingers (sclerodactyly see Fig. 1). Capillaroscopy revealed dilated and distorted capillaries, consistent with early scleroderma. Laboratory tests supported this diagnosis, showing a positive anti-centromere antibody and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). These findings, combined with clinical features such as Raynaud's phenomenon and the onset of gastrointestinal symptoms, confirmed the diagnosis of scleroderma. Consequently, she was started on adalimumab for disease management.Following the initiation of adalimumab, the patient developed a perianal abscess, which was surgically drained and treated with antibiotics. However, her condition continued to deteriorate, with the development of rectal bleeding and a perianal fistula. A colonoscopy revealed gastrointestinal involvement consistent with systemic sclerosis, leading to a modification in her treatment regimen to include methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and hydroxychloroquine.Several months later, the patient began experiencing symptoms consistent with ankylosing spondylitis, such as persistent lower back pain and sacroiliac joint tenderness. MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed active sacroiliitis. Around the same time, she developed hypertension, likely secondary to systemic sclerosis, and was started on antihypertensive therapy.As her disease continued to progress, the patient exhibited signs consistent with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), including a malar rash, oral ulcers, and photosensitivity. Laboratory tests revealed a positive anti-dsDNA antibody and low complement levels (C3 and C4), further supporting the diagnosis of SLE. She was started on hydroxychloroquine and low-dose corticosteroids, with careful monitoring for any signs of lupus nephritis or other organ involvement.Despite these interventions, the patient's condition worsened, with recurrent episodes of vertigo, headaches, dizziness, diarrhea, and fever. A comprehensive reevaluation, including repeat imaging and laboratory tests, indicated ongoing systemic inflammation and muscle weakness, raising concerns for polymyositis. Creatine kinase levels were elevated, and an electromyography study showed evidence of myopathic changes, leading to a diagnosis of polymyositis. Her treatment was adjusted to include high-dose corticosteroids and azathioprine to manage the polymyositis.The combination of systemic sclerosis, SLE, and polymyositis—often collectively referred to as overlap syndrome—complicated the patient's clinical picture. As her disease progressed, she developed additional complications, including interstitial lung disease, confirmed by chest X-ray and CT scan (see Fig. 2), and further gastrointestinal issues which revealed by the axial CT scan that she has small sliding hiatal hernia (see Fig. 3). Blood tests showed elevated inflammatory markers and positive anti-Scl-70 antibodies, confirming the diagnosis of systemic sclerosis, while CCP antibodies were negative, ruling out concurrent rheumatoid arthritis.Over time, the patient's functional status declined significantly. She reported increasing limitations in her daily activities due to persistent joint pain, muscle weakness, stiffness, and fatigue, which had a profound impact on her quality of life. Her care was managed through a multidisciplinary approach, with regular follow-ups to monitor disease activity using tools like the modified Rodnan skin score, BASDAI score, and muscle strength assessments.In the most recent phase of her illness, despite aggressive management with infliximab infusions, methotrexate, and corticosteroids, the patient's condition remains severe and chronic. She frequently presents to the ER with symptoms such as productive cough, shortness of breath, and exacerbations of systemic sclerosis and SLE. Her condition is further complicated by recurrent lower limb swelling, pain, and cellulitis, requiring hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics.The prognosis for the patient is guarded due to the progressive nature of her autoimmune conditions. Future management will focus on controlling disease progression while mitigating the risks of potential complications such as worsening pulmonary involvement, renal crisis, and further gastrointestinal issues. The care team is prepared to adjust her treatment plan as needed, balancing the need for disease control with the management of medication-related side effects.

Discussion

A rare systemic autoimmune disease known as mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD) has characteristics with at least 2 other connective tissue diseases (CTD), such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc), polymyositis (PM), dermatomyositis (DM), and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). It is also characterized by the presence of a unique antibody called anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein (RNP), formerly known as an antibody to extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) [2]. There is significant inter-individual variance in the clinical presentations of MCTD, and the condition lacks distinctive clinical features. The Alarcon-Segovia diagnostic criteria, which include 3 or more of the following clinical symptoms hand Edema, acrosclerosis, myositis with histological confirmation, synovitis, and Raynaud syndrome, and a high titter of positive anti-U1-RNP (above 1 per 1600), is one that is frequently used [3].Uncertainty regarding the cause of mixed connective tissue disease. Thus yet, no distinct risk factor has been found. In persons with a genetic predisposition, environmental variables are likely to play a role in immune activation. It has been discovered that the illness is associated with specific viruses and substances [4].The exact incidence of mixed connective tissue disease is unknown, making it a rare condition. Population-based research conducted in Olmsted County, Minnesota, found that there were 1.9 cases of MCTD for every 100,000 adults annually. About 84% of the affected populations were female, and the mean age at diagnosis was 48 years [5]. This disease affects all races, and its clinical manifestations are similar in all ethnic groups.Even while mixed connective tissue disease was once thought to be a benign and treatable ailment, it can frequently be fatal. A third of patients with MCTD may experience life-threatening consequences, but the remaining nearly one-third experience complete remission. The prognosis is based on the organ involved, the level of inflammation, and how quickly the illness is progressing. There is a range of 8 to 36% for the death rate [6].Anti-U1 RNP is the most significant serology in (MCTD); however, a variety of other serology tests can also be positive in MCTD, such as ANA, which is positive in all MCTD patients. Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, which are positive in 50% of MCTD patients, and rheumatoid factor, which is positive in 70% of MCTD patients. Anti-Sm, anti-double-stranded DNA, anti-Ro/SS-A, and anti-single-stranded DNA tests are additional ones that can test positive for MCTD [7].For MCTD, there is no specific treatment available. For mild to moderate symptoms, however, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, corticosteroids, and anti-malaria medications like hydroxychloroquine are the preferred treatments. If the kidneys or central nervous system are among the internal organs affected, immunosuppression with drugs such as cyclophosphamide is necessary [8,9].

Conclusion

Finally, this MCTD case illustrates the complexity of managing a condition that defies straightforward categorization and treatment. The patient's experience reflects the unpredictable nature of MCTD, where overlapping symptoms of systemic sclerosis, SLE, and polymyositis converge, leading to a cascade of severe complications despite aggressive management. The presence of specific serological markers like anti-U1RNP antibodies, alongside evolving clinical symptoms, underscores the need for early and accurate diagnosis. This case highlights that, while MCTD may initially present with manageable symptoms, its progression can be relentless and life-altering, necessitating a vigilant and adaptable treatment approach. The ongoing challenge lies in balancing symptom control with the prevention of further organ damage, all within the framework of a disease that remains enigmatic in both cause and course.

Ethics approval

Our institution does not require ethical approval for reporting individual cases or case series.

Patient consent

Written informed consent was obtained from the patient's Herself for her anonymized information to be published in this article.

PMC11472140.raw_case:
Movement disorders in dengue encephalitis: a case report and literature review
Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease caused by the dengue virus (DENV). The clinical manifestations of DENV infection range from mild febrile illness to severe dengue shock syndrome and dengue hemorrhagic fever. Recently, its neurological manifestations have been reported. The mechanisms of neurological complications in DENV infection are often attributed to neurotropism or may be immune-mediated. A double-doughnut sign is a radiological pattern of signal changes in the bilateral thalami, resembling a doughnut. Although this sign has been reported with dengue encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, and other neurotropic infections, its co-occurrence with mixed movement disorders is rare. We report a case of dengue encephalitis involving a spectrum of movement disorders in the form of jaw opening dystonia, stereotypies, parkinsonism, and tremors during recovery. Magnetic resonance imaging showed bilateral thalami involvement with a double-doughnut sign. The patient was managed with pulse steroid therapy and benzodiazepines and showed gradual improvement in symptoms. Movement disorders with DENV infection are rare and self-limiting. 

Introduction

Dengue encephalitis is a rare neurological complication of dengue fever, caused by dengue virus (DENV). Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical presentation, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, and detection of DENV RNA or antibodies in the serum or cerebrospinal fluid [1]. Movement disorders in dengue encephalitis are rare but can manifest as part of the neurological complications caused by the virus affecting the brain. These disorders may include tremors, myoclonus, chorea, ataxia, and parkinsonism [2]. The exact mechanisms are unclear, but they likely result from direct viral invasion, immune-mediated injury, or metabolic disturbances affecting the basal ganglia and other motor control regions of the brain. Here, in this case report, we are presenting a case of dengue encephalitis who developed a spectrum of movement disorders in the form of jaw opening dystonia, stereotypies, Parkinsonism, and tremors during the course of his recovery

Case Report

A 60-year-old male presenting with a high-grade fever for 5 days was experiencing arthralgia and myalgia. Two days after the onset of fever, the patient developed gradual deterioration in sensorium and could not communicate, although he could comprehend, and he was lethargic on presentation. He had no history of seizures, headaches, or vomiting. On examination, he had hepatomegaly and was delirious, with neck rigidity and a bilateral extensor plantar response.Biochemical parameters revealed raised levels of aspartate aminotransferase (150 IU/L) and alanine aminotransferase (100 IU/L) with thrombocytopenia (80,000/mm3). The patient’s blood sample was sent for a fever panel for malarial parasites, Leptospira immunoglobulin M (IgM), dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) and IgM, and Typhidot IgM. The serum tested positive for the DENV NS1 antigen. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a cell count of 5 cells/µL, a protein level of 92 mg/dL, a glucose level of 60 mg/dL, and an opening pressure of 8 cm H2O. The gram stain was negative for the cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, cryptococcal antigens, and other neurotropic viruses. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed bilateral thalamic involvement with a double-doughnut sign, as in Figure 1 (T1- and T2-weighted MRI). The patient was started on symptomatic treatment with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone, 1 g per day for 5 days. On day 4 of admission, the patient showed spontaneous opening of the eyes and was obeying commands, although he was mildly confused. He had developed jaw-opening dystonia (Supplementary Video 1). He was managed with a benzodiazepine (clonazepam 0.25 mg at bedtime) and tetrabenazine (50 mg in two divided doses). Gradually, his dystonia subsided. After 5 to 6 days, he developed stereotypical kinetic tremor movement of his bilateral upper limbs (left > right) and facial hypomimia. The tetrabenazine was stopped, while treatment with benzodiazepines and low-dose beta blockers was continued. The patient’s symptoms resolved, and he was discharged in stable condition after 2 weeks. Written informed consent for publication of information related to medical condition was obtained from the patient’s attendant.

Discussion

Dengue is an arboviral infection caused by DENV. The neurological manifestations of DENV infection are varied and include encephalitis, myelitis, myositis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, hypokalemic paralysis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, and opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome [1]. Movement disorders have been commonly reported in Japanese encephalitis and less commonly with dengue encephalitis [2]. The double-doughnut sign has been described with dengue encephalitis [3,4], Japanese encephalitis [5], and other neurotropic infections; however, its co-occurrence with dystonia is rare [ 6].We report a case of dengue encephalitis in which the patient developed a spectrum of movement disorders in the form of jaw-opening dystonia, stereotypies, parkinsonism, and tremors during recovery. Dengue is considered an endemic tropical and subtropical arboviral infection caused by the DENV and spread by the mosquito Aedes aegypti. Asia accounts for 70% of the worldwide disease burden. DENV can cause neurological complications and DENV encephalitis, dengue encephalopathy, immune-mediated syndromes, muscle dysfunction, dengue-associated stroke, and neuro-ophthalmic complications [7]. The proposed mechanisms of neurological complications of DENV infection are metabolic alterations or direct viral invasion that includes encephalitis, myositis, meningitis, myelitis, and autoimmune reactions, including acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, neuromyelitis optica, optic neuritis, myelitis, encephalopathy, and Guillain-Barré syndrome [8]. The occurrence rate of movement disorders in dengue encephalitis is reported to be 11%, which includes parkinsonian features [2]. DENV causes direct damage to neurons, leading to cerebral edema and hemorrhage caused by a vascular leakage, which typically affects both sides of the thalamus and basal ganglia and manifests radiologically as the so-called double-doughnut sign [8]. In the present case, dengue encephalitis was diagnosed based on criteria established by Cristiane et al. [9], including the presence of fever, acute signs of cerebral involvement such as altered consciousness or personality and/or seizures and/or focal neurological signs, reactive IgM dengue antibody, NS1 antigen, or positive dengue polymerase chain reaction in serum and/or CSF and the exclusion of other causes of viral encephalitis and encephalopathy. The management of dengue encephalitis is mainly supportive. The patient in this case was administered high-dose steroid therapy (1 g methylprednisolone for 5 days) when he developed dystonia along with other movement disorders. These symptoms responded to symptomatic treatment. MRI showed bilateral thalamic lesions that were hypointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2 (Figure 1), with central blooming suggestive of the double-doughnut sign. The MRI apparent diffusion coefficient scan and diffusion-weighted image are shown in Figure 2. The findings contrast with the indications of Japanese encephalitis, in which the movement disorders appear late and are prolonged with disabling sequelae [2]. That previous case of encephalitis may be attributed to an immune-mediated mechanism, whereas the improvement in the present case could largely be attributed to steroids. The double-doughnut sign with dystonia/parkinsonism was previously reported only in a single case of DENV encephalitis [6].Post-dengue parkinsonism is rare. Extrapyramidal manifestation of dengue has been postulated to be due to its neurotropic effect on basal ganglia. A similar case report from Sri Lanka showed dengue IgM positivity in the CSF of a patient with parkinsonism on day 5 of admission; however, the MRI was normal and portrayed no double-doughnut sign [10]. Moreover, a longitudinal study from Taiwan showed that patients with dengue fever had an increased risk of developing Parkinson disease later in life [11]. Numerous neurotropic viruses have been shown to penetrate the nervous system and cause various forms of encephalopathy/encephalitis, with parkinsonism a probable manifestation. However, it remains unclear how these viruses cause parkinsonism. Repeated attempts to isolate viral particles in the brain or antibodies in the serum or CSF of Parkinson disease patients have failed [12].Early identification and prompt symptomatic treatment of dengue encephalitis are crucial for a satisfactory clinical outcome. Further studies are needed to elucidate the mechanism of neurological manifestation in dengue infection.

PMC11563655.raw_case:
Conjunctival Phlyctenule and Nodular Scleritis in a Patient with Previous Herpes Simplex Virus-2 Exposure: Causative Agent or Innocent Bystander?


Abstract



Introduction

Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is an inflammatory condition arising from a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, presenting with inflamed nodules on the conjunctiva and cornea. Scleritis is a severe ocular inflammation linked to systemic diseases, potentially vision threatening, and involving immune responses similar to phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis. This case report discusses a patient with a history of herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 infection who primarily developed phlyctenular conjunctivitis and later progressed to nodular scleritis.

Case Presentation

A 66-year-old female presented with pain, redness, and a foreign body sensation in her left eye for 2 days. Initial treatment for epidemic keratoconjunctivitis with tobramycin-dexamethasone improved her symptoms. However, 3 weeks later, she developed a conjunctival phlyctenule. Diagnostic tests, including blood work and conjunctival swabs, were conducted. While most tests were negative, HSV-2 IgG was positive. The patient failed topical corticosteroid monotherapy; however, she responded to oral valacyclovir. Follow-up examinations showed significant improvement, with resolution of the conjunctival phlyctenule and nodular scleritis, and her best-corrected visual acuity returned to 20/20.

Conclusion

This case highlights the importance of considering HSV-2 in atypical presentations of phlyctenular conjunctivitis and scleritis. The patient’s response to antiviral therapy underscores the potential role of HSV-2 in such ocular inflammation. Thorough infectious workups and alternative treatment approaches are crucial in managing unconventional cases. Experimental treatments based on laboratory findings can be valuable for patients preferring conservative management, emphasizing the need for close follow-up and personalized care in ocular inflammatory diseases.

Introduction

Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis (PKC) is an inflammatory condition that is believed to result from a type IV hypersensitivity reaction to antigens [1, 2]. PKC is marked by the presence of inflamed nodules on the conjunctiva and cornea [3]. Conjunctival phlyctenae are usually temporary and cause mild to moderate symptoms [4].Scleritis is a severe ocular pathology characterized by inflammation of the sclera [5]. It is potentially vision threatening and is associated with systemic conditions, which are often life threatening [6]. Although the pathogenesis is not completely understood, it is similar to PKC in that it may result from immune complex deposition or local delayed hypersensitivity reactions [7]. In this case report, we discuss a case of a patient who presented with phlyctenular conjunctivitis and nodular scleritis with a strong past medical history of herpes simplex virus (HSV)-2 infection.

Case Presentation

A 66-year-old female presented to our urgent clinic with complaints of pain, redness, and a foreign body sensation in her left eye (OS) for 2 days. Her past medical history was irrelevant. Her best-corrected vision acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 and 20/25 in the right eye and OS. Upon slit lamp examination (SLE) on the left eye, mild chemosis, diffuse conjunctival injection, mild mucoid discharge, and follicular reaction in palpebral conjunctiva were observed. The rest of SLE and dilated fundoscopic exam in both eyes were normal. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes, and relative afferent pupillary defect was negative. Given epidemic keratoconjunctivitis as the first diagnosis, she was prescribed tobramycin-dexamethasone ophthalmic drop four times a day OS. A week later, she reported improvement in her symptoms of OS. SLE showed significant improvement as well. At this time, tobramycin-dexamethasone ophthalmic drop was tapered by one drop per week. She was advised to return if any problems persisted during the tapering process or within 1 week after completely discontinuing the eye drop.Approximately 3 weeks later, while she was still on the eye drop twice a day, she came back reporting a lesion on the inferotemporal conjunctiva with pain and significant redness OS. Her BCVA was 20/40 (OS). SLE confirmed an elevated lesion inside conjunctiva (shown in Fig. 1a, b). She was diagnosed with conjunctival phlyctenule. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) (shown in Fig. 1c) and ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) (shown in Fig. 1d) of the area confirmed the diagnosis of conjunctival phlyctenule OS. The following blood work, including complete blood count and differentiation, comprehensive metabolic profile, human leukocyte antigen-B27, C-reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibody, anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic antibody, rapid plasma reagin, florescent treponemal antibody-absorption, QuantiFERON TB gold, Lyme Western blot, Bartonella IgG and IgM, angiotensin-converting enzyme, lysozyme, rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclitic citrullinated peptide, varicella-zoster virus IgG and IgM, HSV-1 and HSV-2 IgG and IgM, and Epstein-Barr virus polymerase chain reaction were ordered. Additionally, conjunctival swabs for HSV-1, HSV-2, and adenovirus were obtained. Tobramycin-dexamethasone was stopped, and the patient was started on prednisolone acetate ophthalmic drop OS every 4 h.During follow-up visit a week later, there was improvement in symptoms; however, the lesion was more prominent, and the patient’s BCVA was 20/30 (OS) (shown in Fig. 2a, b). All laboratory tests, including conjunctival polymerase chain reactions, came back negative except for a positive HSV-2 IgG result. After discussing diagnostic biopsy versus experimental treatment for HSV-2 along with their pros and cons, she decided to proceed with conservative management. Valacyclovir was started at a dose of 1 g three times a day, while prednisolone was started to taper. Two weeks later, SLE demonstrated impressive improvement in the size and elevation of the conjunctival lesions; however, a deep cystic lesion with turbid fluid was observed, and the patient’s BCVA was 20/20 (OS) (shown in Fig. 3a–c). Nodular scleritis OS as demonstrated by an anterior segment OCT is shown in Figure 3d–l in contrast with the first time. She was advised to continue valacyclovir 1 g daily and prednisolone acetate ophthalmic drop twice per day in the left eye.Three weeks later, her symptoms had been completely resolved and SLE showed near-complete resolution of conjunctival phlyctenule and nodular scleritis with slightly thinning of the area (shown in Fig. 4a–c). The patient’s BCVA was 20/20 (OS). As a result, her treatment regimen then consisted of continuing 1 g of valacyclovir daily for at least a year, tapering prednisolone from once daily for 2 weeks to once every other day for another 2 weeks before complete discontinuation. She was asked to come back in 3 months for a follow-up visit or sooner with any aggravation. At her last visit, 8 months after starting antiviral therapy, she is still doing fine without any flare-ups. The plan is to continue systemic antiviral therapy for 1 year.The written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the use of her information, images, and paraclinical test results. The CARE Checklist has been completed by the authors for this case report, attached as online supplementary material (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000542076).

Discussion

PKC can be associated with HSV, but it usually occurs as part of the initial HSV infection, accompanied by vesicular blepharokeratoconjunctivitis [1, 8, 9]. The primary treatment for PKC focuses on reducing inflammation [2]. Alongside managing inflammation, it is crucial to address the antigen sources causing the reaction, often by treating the associated underlying pathology. For patients with infectious diseases, treating the underlying infections is essential.Infectious scleritis (IS) is a condition not widely discussed outside of ophthalmologic literature, where it is reported to occur in approximately 5%–18% of scleritis cases [7]. If the pain is disproportionate to the physical findings, an infectious cause should be considered. IS can be caused by bacteria, fungi, parasites, and viruses [10]. The literature describes several cases in which patients have presented with scleritis secondary to a herpetic origin [11–13]. Literature suggests that herpetic scleritis can be suspected in a patient with unilateral, sudden-onset anterior scleritis, which is generally accompanied by moderate to intense pain [14]. Diagnosing IS can be challenging due to its similarity to autoimmune scleritis, the most common form of the condition [7]. A detailed patient history is crucial, as most cases have an identifiable trigger prior to symptom onset [8]. Patients with IS, especially secondary to HSV, generally respond well to oral corticosteroids and antiviral treatment [12, 13, 15].Although herpes virus has been reported as a causative agent of scleritis, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first case report of a patient who initially presented with conjunctival phlyctenule that subsequently progressed to nodular scleritis on topical corticosteroid therapy with probable HSV-2 infection as an underlying etiology. In our case, subsequent scleral involvement may be attributed to employing topical steroids without antiviral coverage in the beginning. Furthermore, unlike what is commonly reported in the literature, our patient’s laboratory test results did not indicate a primary herpes infection (IgM negative). We were unable to confirm HSV-2 as the underlying pathogen because the patient did not consent to the procedure. However, her impressive response to anti-HSV therapy provides indirect evidence supporting this diagnosis.It is important to highlight that our patient was diagnosed with a conjunctival phlyctenule, which is different from limbal and corneal phlyctenules [16, 17]. This condition can arise exclusively in the conjunctiva and may resolve without leaving any scars. This was supported by anterior OCT and UBM results, which showed no scleral involvement in Figure 1. Furthermore, she later developed nodular scleritis during the course of her illness, as confirmed by UBM in Figure 3.In our patient, the initial presentation was acute viral conjunctivitis; however, the symptoms returned in 3 weeks with conjunctival phlyctenule. The presence of HSV-2 IgG, along with the absence of HSV-2 IgM and a negative HSV-2 conjunctival swab test, reduces the likelihood of an acute infection with HSV-2. On the other hand, not responding to frequent topical corticosteroid monotherapy along with an impressive response to anti-HSV antiviral therapy confirms that our patient had an infectious component with HSV-2.We may face criticism for concluding that our patient responded more to antiviral therapy than topical corticosteroid therapy. Given the lack of significant change in the lesion size and shape with the topical corticosteroid ophthalmic drops for a week and the addition of valacyclovir at a dose of 1 g three times a day along with tapering prednisolone acetate, the response is more likely due to the valacyclovir rather than topical corticosteroid therapy.The primary limitation of our case report is the absence of a conjunctival and/or scleral biopsy, with treatment decisions based primarily on laboratory tests. While we acknowledge this limitation, it is important to note that biopsy was discussed with the patient, who ultimately declined the procedure. A further limitation of our study was the lack of follow-up IgG titer testing after 4 weeks, which would have provided evidence of seroconversion.Considering herpes causes about 5–7% of scleritis cases, this case highlights the importance of conducting a thorough diagnostic infectious workup, especially in unique or unconventional presentations such as seen in this case report [13, 14]. In addition, this case also emphasizes the importance of considering an alternate approach in unconventional cases of conjunctival phlyctenule and nodular scleritis with close follow-up.In conclusion, HSV-2 should be considered in unconventional cases of conjunctival phlyctenule and nodular scleritis. Moreover, experimental treatment based on laboratory findings can be considered as an alternative approach for patients who prefer conservative management.

Statement of Ethics

Ethics approval was not required in accordance with local guidelines and the University of Florida Intuitional Review Board. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of the details of their medical case and any accompanying images.

Conflict of Interest Statement

The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare.

Funding Sources

This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

Author Contributions

Shawn Khan, Khushi Saigal, and Arash Maleki: conception and design of the study, data analysis and interpretation, drafting of the manuscript, and approval of the final version of the manuscript.
